sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse singulation (picking an individual product from ... of many items and placing it in a tray). Removing a specific flagged consumer object (bottle, knife, tool) from a divest tray or opened bag and depositing it in a disposal receptacle is the same perception-and-grasp problem: same object classes, sizes and weights, no fine precision, conveyor-fed presentation.

sources.title: AMP's Horowitz on Bringing AI to the Recycling World (Waste360 Q&A)
sources.claim: AMP's Cortex robotic sorters run commercially in material recovery facilities, picking targeted item classes out of a moving stream of mixed clutter at 80-120 picks per minute with up ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic waste sortation. Recognising a targeted class of object in a heterogeneous conveyor-borne stream, grasping it and diverting it to a separate container is functionally the confiscation-and-disposal step, at higher throughput and with at least as much object variety as checkpoint surrender items.

sources.system: Mechanical Search (Dex-Net-based policies on an ABB YuMi)
sources.title: Mechanical Search: Multi-Step Retrieval of a Target Object Occluded by Clutter (arXiv:1903.01588)
sources.claim: Research robots autonomously locate and extract a known target object buried under a heap of distractor objects in a bin, succeeding in over 95% of trials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: retrieving a designated object occluded by clutter in a fixtured bin, which is what pulling a flagged bottle or knife out of an opened, presented bag requires. Demonstrated only in a lab workcell with rigid objects in a bin, so it supports an E1 presentation, not an as-found packed suitcase.

sources.title: Learning to Open Deformable Bags with a Bimanual Robot (UCB/EECS-2025-111)
sources.claim: Opening a closed, deformable bag is still a research problem for bimanual robots, studied in lab settings rather than deployed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: opening a closed bag before reaching inside. Cited as the state of the art for the unzipping/opening step of a checked-bag search; it is a laboratory demonstration, so it does not substantiate worker-quality opening of arbitrary passenger luggage.

sources.developer: San Jose Mineta International Airport (vendor deployment)
sources.title: Humanoid robot Jose deployed at US airport to improve passenger experience
sources.claim: Airport-deployed humanoid/service robots handle wayfinding and passenger information; none is reported taking custody of passengers' prohibited items at a checkpoint.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: passenger-facing information delivery in an airport concourse. Shows what human-facing airport robots actually do (directions and information) and that no cited system conducts the item-surrender or advisory transaction, supporting the negative judgments at E2.

tasks.label: Provide directions and respond to passenger inquiries.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Direct passengers to areas where they can pick up their baggage after screening is complete.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: View images of checked bags and cargo, using remote screening equipment, and alert baggage screeners or handlers to any possible problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Locate suspicious bags pictured in printouts sent from remote monitoring areas, and set these bags aside for inspection.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-line checked baggage screening: a remote on-screen-resolution operator in a separate room flags a bag whose EDS image alarms and sends the image; the screener in the checked baggage resolution area (CBRA) identifies the alarmed bag arriving/queued on the conveyor line and pulls it onto a search table for ETD/hand inspection.

Passenger checkpoint carry-on: the X-ray/remote image operator flags a bag; the screener at the exit rollers must pick the correct bag or bin out of the several emerging from the tunnel and move it to the secondary search table, keeping the rest of the line moving.

Bag that has left the tracked flow: a printed image arrives for a bag already sorted downstream, sitting on a cart, stacked in the make-up area or on a carousel, or staged at a stand-alone screening setup in a small airport lobby; the screener must visually match the picture against many loose bags and extract the right one.

Air cargo, mail, or oversize/odd-size baggage screening facility: an image of a flagged skid, carton, or oversize item is sent from the screening room; the screener locates that piece among freight staged on pallets or in the oversize area of the warehouse and sets it aside for physical inspection.

sources.system: Daifuku Mobile Inspection Table (MIT) AGV fleet
sources.developer: Daifuku Airport Technologies / Jervis B. Webb
sources.title: What's in Your Bag? New Screening and Tracking Technology Make for Safer Airways
sources.claim: Daifuku's Mobile Inspection Tables — AGV robots deployed in the CBRA at Miami International (102 units) — receive alarmed checked bags automatically off the belt conveyor and drive them into the TSA search room, i.e., the flagged bag is set aside for inspection without a screener locating or lifting it.

sources.title: Helping Reduce Staff Workload at US Airports with the "MIT" AGV-Based Inspection Table
sources.claim: The MIT system uses AGVs to move baggage flagged for further inspection to the inspection station in US airport checked baggage resolution areas; Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport was the first US adopter.

sources.system: Automated Screening Lanes (ASL) with automatic alarm-bin divert
sources.developer: TSA with Delta / Vanderlande-Scarabee, Smiths Detection
sources.title: TSA, Delta jointly launch automated screening checkpoint lanes at LaGuardia Airport
sources.claim: TSA Automated Screening Lanes, deployed at US checkpoints (LaGuardia, Las Vegas, Denver, New Orleans), automatically push any carry-on bag/bin that alarms onto a separate conveyor and area for secondary inspection, with RFID tags and bin-content cameras linked to the X-ray image.

sources.title: 12 cool facts about the AI-powered robots that help deliver your Amazon packages
sources.claim: Amazon's Robin robotic arm uses vision to segment, identify and locate individual packages in a mixed flow on a conveyor and picks the targeted package onto a drive unit routed to the right destination; it has handled over a billion packages.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: selecting one identified item out of a mixed, uncontrolled flow of parcels on a belt and moving it to a separate destination. Same perception-plus-pick-and-place problem, comparable object sizes, weights and irregular shapes to carry-on bags and cartons, in an institution-run facility.

sources.title: Towards a fully automated baggage hall - Vanderlande
sources.claim: Robotic baggage loading — vision-guided arms that grip and stack individual suitcases from the baggage handling system into containers — has been operational for many ..., showing that robots reliably manipulate real passenger luggage inside airport baggage halls.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: gripping and moving individual passenger bags of arbitrary shape, weight and surface within an airport baggage hall — the same physical handling required to pull a flagged bag off the line and place it on an inspection table.

sources.title: First US tote-based baggage system goes live
sources.claim: BEUMER's CrisBag tote-based independent carrier system, TSA-approved for in-tote screening and live at San Francisco Airport, keeps 100% track-and-trace of every bag and routes alarmed bags directly to CBRA inspection stations, eliminating manual re-routing and handling.

roles.title: School Bus Monitors
aliases: SPED Bus Aide (Special Ed Bus Aide)
SPED Bus Paraeducator (Special Education Bus Paraeducator)
SPED School Bus Monitor (Special Education School Bus Monitor)
roles.description: Maintain order among students on a school bus. Duties include helping students safely board and exit and communicating behavioral problems. May perform pretrip and posttrip inspections and prepare for and assist in emergency evacuations.

tasks.label: Buckle seatbelts or fasten wheelchair tie-down straps to secure passengers for transportation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Special-needs or pre-K route bus: at each curbside stop the monitor buckles an ambulatory young student into a standard bus bench seat with a lap or lap-shoulder belt — reaching across the seated child, routing webbing over a winter coat or backpack, inserting the tongue into the buckle at the hip, and cinching it snug in a narrow aisle within 20-30 seconds per child.

Small child or student with disabilities placed in a child safety restraint system (integrated child seat, safety vest, or star/harness seat): the monitor threads a 5-point harness over shoulders and between legs, adjusts shoulder-strap height and tension to that child's body, and connects the vest's cam-wrap straps to the seat back and seat anchors.

Wheelchair-seated student on a lift-equipped special-needs bus who cannot secure themselves: monitor positions the chair forward-facing over the floor track, hooks four retractor straps to designated frame points on that particular wheelchair model, tensions them, then buckles and adjusts the anchored lap-and-shoulder occupant belt on the child.

Older, self-directing power-wheelchair student who drives their own chair into the securement area and can manage their own occupant belt; what the monitor must do is secure the mobility device itself to the vehicle before departure.

Student who resists or repeatedly releases the restraint: the monitor re-buckles a squirming, sometimes combative or self-injurious student, often after the bus pulls over mid-route, using calming and behavior-management judgment and sometimes a specialized restraint or buckle guard.

Pre-departure securement check from front to back of a loaded bus: verify every student's belt or harness is fastened and correctly routed (not behind the back, twisted, or under the arm), tighten loose belts and re-buckle any that were released, then signal the driver to depart.

sources.system: QUANTUM automatic rear-facing wheelchair securement station
sources.date: 2013 launch; Gen II 2020; product page updated 2022
sources.title: Q'STRAINT: QUANTUM Automatic Rear-Facing Wheelchair Securement System
sources.claim: Q'STRAINT QUANTUM is a commercially sold automatic wheelchair securement station whose motorized, sensor-equipped arms grip and hold a wheelchair inside a bus without any worker attaching straps; it is offered for city and coach buses and the US backrest carries an integrated lap-and-shoulder belt that the passenger fastens.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: securing a mobility device to a bus floor for transport. It substitutes for the monitor's four-point tie-down work on comparable objects (passenger wheelchairs and scooters) inside a bus interior; it does not, however, fasten a belt on the occupant.

sources.developer: Q'STRAINT with AAATA and UMTRI (MDOT Michigan Mobility Challenge)
sources.title: Autonomous Wheelchair Securement — Michigan Department of Transportation
sources.claim: QUANTUM units are in revenue service on public transit buses: ten buses on TheRide's fixed routes in Ann Arbor-Ypsilanti were fitted with the system, replacing manual driver securement of wheelchairs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: attendant/driver securement of a wheelchair for transport. Same object class and the same vehicle-interior environment as the school-bus tie-down instance; the device performs the securement the worker would otherwise do by hand.

sources.title: Q'Straint Quantum Now Available to Order | Mass Transit
sources.claim: The securement sequence runs without the vehicle operator leaving the driver's seat and completes in under 25 seconds, i.e. no worker performs the strap-fastening step.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task (wheelchair securement for transport); establishes that the machine, not a human attendant, performs the securement in normal service.

sources.system: FMVSS 222 wheelchair securement requirement (regulatory constraint, not a robot)
sources.date: rule from 1992; article December 2008; standard still current
sources.title: The Dos and Don'ts of Wheelchair Transport Safety — School Bus Fleet
sources.claim: US school buses must have forward-facing wheelchair stations with four-point strap-type securement, so the rear-facing automatic station deployed in transit buses is not an applicable substitute for the school-bus wheelchair instance as those buses are built.
sources.transferJustification: Context for the negative judgments: it constrains which automated securement hardware would produce an accepted output on a US school bus.

sources.developer: academic authors, IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
sources.title: A High-Strength, Highly-Flexible Robotic Strap for Harnessing, Lifting, and Transferring Humans | IEEE Xplore
sources.claim: Robotic manipulation of straps around a human body remains an open research problem; a 2023 IEEE paper presents a laboratory 'Robotic Strap' for harnessing and lifting people and describes the problem as unsolved for current robots.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: routing and tensioning a strap around a seated person's body — the core motion of buckling a child's belt or harness. Cited only as lab-stage evidence; it does not support completion at any tier.

tasks.label: Escort young children across roads or highways.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood residential two-lane road stop: monitor steps off the bus first with the stop arm and red lights activated, checks both directions for traffic, signals 2-6 elementary students to cross in front of the bus, holds the hands of the youngest, keeps the group together, and confirms all reach the far curb before releasing the bus.

Higher-speed rural highway or multi-lane arterial stop: 45-55 mph traffic, limited sightlines, drivers who illegally pass the stopped bus; monitor must judge gaps, hold children physically back at the edge of the road, use a hand signal or stop paddle, and abort and restart the crossing when a vehicle does not stop.

Special-needs route: escorting a preschool or disabled child (wheelchair/walker, autism, elopement risk) across the street from the bus to a waiting parent at the curb or door, including physical support, hand-holding, and verified hand-off to the adult.

On school grounds at arrival/dismissal: escorting groups of young children across the bus loop or staff parking driveway between the bus line and the building doors, with marked crosswalks, slow-moving school traffic and school staff controlling the premises.

Adverse conditions: dark winter morning or dusk, rain/snow/ice/fog, snowbanks and slush at the curb; a child darts ahead or drops a backpack or paper in the roadway and the monitor must physically restrain the child or retrieve the item while traffic is stopped.

sources.developer: Hovannes Kulhandjian, Fresno State / Mineta Transportation Institute
sources.title: Researcher designs robot to help children cross streets safely (Tech Xplore)
sources.claim: CrossBot, a university research prototype crossing-guard robot, rolls into a crosswalk and displays a red/green screen to tell children when it is safe to ...; it is a video-demonstration prototype that signals rather than physically escorting children, with no documented school deployment.
sources.transferJustification: Closest system to the task (child street crossing), but it only signals from the crosswalk; it does not lead, hold, restrain or account for a group of young children, and it remains an unfielded prototype, so it does not substantiate completion at any tier.

sources.title: Towson University rolls out Starship Technologies' food delivery robots
sources.claim: Starship's sidewalk delivery robots operate commercially and autonomously on public sidewalks and campuses, including unaided road crossings at very large scale, but they carry cargo and traverse crossings alone; they do not accompany, control or protect pedestrians.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is autonomous street crossing by a small mobile robot. Capability does not transfer: the robot crosses only itself, has no means of taking custody of children, and its risk model tolerates its own delay or collision, unlike escorting children.

sources.system: Autonomous navigation robot for visually impaired people (field trial)
sources.title: Field Trials of Autonomous Navigation Robot for Visually Impaired People
sources.claim: Field trials of an autonomous guide robot that leads a single adult visually impaired user report that curbs and street crossings were the lowest-rated aspects, indicating that human-guiding robots in traffic remain at research-trial maturity with a cooperative adult in the loop.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is a robot physically guiding a person across a street. It does not transfer: the guided party is a cooperative harness-holding adult, the trials are research-stage, and crossings were the weakest-performing element - far from escorting unpredictable young children.

tasks.label: Assist children with disabilities or children with psychological, emotional, or behavioral issues with boarding and exiting the school bus.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential curbside/driveway stop: an ambulatory student with a physical or developmental disability boards/exits the bus. Monitor steps down first, offers a hand or arm for balance on the steep steps and handrail, carries the backpack, watches for passing traffic, guides the student to the assigned seat and buckles a standard belt.

Residential stop, wheelchair student: monitor deploys/positions the student's manual or power chair onto the bus's power lift, rides or guides it up, maneuvers the chair into the securement position inside the aisle, applies four-point tiedowns and lap/shoulder occupant restraint, and reverses the process at the home stop, handing the student to a caregiver.

School bus loading zone at arrival/dismissal, wheelchair student: same lift-and-tiedown sequence performed on paved school property with staff present, fixed loading lanes, and a queue of buses on schedule.

Student with autism or emotional/behavioral issues who resists boarding or exiting at a curbside stop: refuses the steps, attempts to elope toward the street, may drop to the ground or become agitated; monitor uses verbal prompts, a visual/routine cue, hand-holding or light physical guidance, then secures the student in a harness-type child safety restraint.

School loading zone dismissal, mixed group: monitor assists several students with disabilities in sequence off the bus (some with crutches/walkers, some needing a steadying hand), keeps them from wandering between buses, and releases each to the correct staff member, in rain, snow or heat.

Preschool/small special-needs child at a home stop: monitor lifts or carries the child up the bus steps, places them in a car seat or safety-vest child restraint system, threads and tightens the harness, and at exit lifts the child down to a waiting parent, confirming the handoff.

sources.title: Q'Straint Introduces Revolutionary New Fully Automatic Wheelchair Securement System - School Transportation News
sources.claim: Q'STRAINT QUANTUM is an automatic rear-facing wheelchair securement station installed in buses; it clamps a mobility device after the passenger has already boarded and positioned the chair themselves and presses a button. It automates only the tiedown sub-step and presumes a self-propelling, cooperative rider — it does not board, lift, guide, or supervise a child.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: securing a wheelchair aboard a transit vehicle, the tiedown portion of this task. It does not transfer to the whole instance because it requires the rider to board and position the chair unaided and provides no assistance to a child who cannot self-navigate or self-regulate.

sources.title: WHILL - Winnipeg Airports Authority
sources.claim: WHILL autonomous wheelchairs self-drive passengers between fixed points inside airport terminals; passengers board and alight the chair themselves and the empty chair returns automatically. This is autonomous passenger transport in a controlled facility, not assistance with boarding a vehicle or care of a child with disabilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: moving a seated mobility-device user through a facility. It does not transfer: the rider must transfer in and out unaided, the routes are pre-mapped indoor concourses, and no step-climbing, lifting, tiedown, or behavioral supervision of a child is involved.

sources.title: PTR Robots Introduces World's First Mobile Lifting Robot That Both Transfers and Rehabilitates Patients | Business Wire
sources.claim: The PTR Robot is a mobile lifting robot for transferring and mobilising patients in hospitals and nursing homes; it is driven and commanded by a caregiver rather than operating autonomously, and is designed for adult patients ... care facilities, not for boarding vehicles or handling children with behavioral issues.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physically lifting/supporting a person. Does not transfer: the machine is operator-driven throughout (continuous human control), works on flat indoor floors with cooperative adults, and cannot substitute for an attendant guiding a child up bus steps.

tasks.label: Monitor the conduct of students to maintain discipline and safety.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Evacuate students from the school bus in emergency situations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled emergency evacuation drill held on school property (required about twice a year in most states): monitor opens/holds the front service door, directs 30-60 K-8 students to leave belongings, moves them out single file, steadies small children on the steps, leads them 100 feet away, takes a head count, and reports. Time target under two minutes.

Real roadside evacuation of ambulatory students during a route for smoke, fuel odor, overheating, or a stalled bus on a public road or highway shoulder: monitor decides the safe side, opens the door, keeps frightened students in line, gets everyone off past traffic, escorts them over a curb/ditch to a safe assembly point, counts heads, and holds the group until a relief bus arrives.

Evacuation of a special-needs bus (drill or real): monitor releases child safety restraint harnesses, star buckles and wheelchair tie-downs, carries or drags non-ambulatory students out on an evacuation blanket or via the rear door, manages oxygen/medical equipment and students with autism or seizure disorders who may resist or bolt, and accounts for every rider.

Crash or fire: bus tipped, struck, or burning with the service door blocked; monitor forces the rear emergency door, side emergency exit windows, or roof hatch, extracts injured and unconscious students, hands children down the rear-door drop to the ground, keeps them clear of fire and traffic, and searches the bus to confirm no one is left aboard.

Rear-door and side/roof-exit drill on school property with older students: monitor positions at the rear door, latches it open, hands or lowers students down the roughly three-foot drop by the wrists, coaches the sit-and-slide technique, prevents jumping injuries, and marshals the group to the assembly point for a count.

sources.system: Robot-guided evacuation research platforms (Penn State Robot Ethics and Aerial Vehicles Lab)
sources.developer: Alan R. Wagner, Pennsylvania State University
sources.title: Robot-Guided Evacuation as a Paradigm for Human-Robot Interaction Research (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: Robot-guided emergency evacuation of people remains a research paradigm studied in laboratory and simulation settings; the author argues real-world experiments with real robots during real emergencies are still needed, and the robots discussed guide or inform evacuees rather than physically handling them.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task: leading people out of a hazardous space. It does not transfer to bus evacuation, which additionally requires opening emergency exits, releasing harnesses, lifting and lowering children, and verifying an empty vehicle; the cited work is lab/simulation only and involves no physical handling of evacuees.

sources.title: TrackReitar Rescue robots - LeoTronics Robotics
sources.claim: A tracked rescue robot marketed for battlefield and disaster casualty removal is described as able to evacuate a person, but it is a remotely piloted tracked vehicle for a single injured adult on open terrain, with no demonstrated autonomous handling of multiple children inside a vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: casualty extraction. It does not transfer: the platform is remotely operated, moves one prone adult over open ground, and cannot enter a bus aisle, release harnesses, or manage a group of ambulatory children.

sources.title: Emergency Rescue - DEEP Robotics
sources.claim: Quadruped robots sold for emergency response deliver supplies and gather situational information for rescuers; they do not move or physically assist people out of danger.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot operation inside an emergency scene. Capability does not carry over: the robot's contribution is logistics and reconnaissance, not opening exits, handling children, or accounting for evacuees.

sources.system: n/a - human work procedure cited only for setting classification
sources.title: Administrative Procedure 3541.35 - Evacuation of School Buses
sources.claim: Task-context source establishing that school bus evacuation drills are conducted on school property under school supervision twice each year, using rear-door and front-door procedures.
sources.transferJustification: Not robotic evidence; cited only to fix the setting of the drill instances (school property, institution-controlled) for setting_tier classification.

tasks.label: Direct students boarding and exiting the school bus.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine neighborhood route stop (K-8 riders): monitor stands at the entry door or steps to the curb, scans the roadway and the bus's 'danger zone', signals students when it is safe to approach, keeps them out of the street, steadies small children on the high steps, hands up backpacks/instruments, counts riders and confirms nobody is under or behind the bus before the driver pulls away. Rain, snow, dark mornings, uneven curbs, parents and pets at the stop.

Special-needs / pre-K route (a large share of monitor assignments): monitor deploys or oversees the wheelchair lift, guides or physically supports students with autism, mobility or behavioral needs up and down the steps and along the aisle, secures wheelchairs, harnesses and car seats, and releases each child hand-to-hand at the door only to an approved parent/aide, refusing release if no one is present.

Arrival/dismissal in the school bus loop: 10-40 buses staged on school property with staff supervision; monitor stands at the door directing students to unload in order, keeps them from walking between buses, points loading students to the correct bus, holds back the line until the aisle clears, and does the final walk-through sweep before departure.

Field trip or activity/athletic trip loading at an off-site destination (museum lot, stadium, park curb): unfamiliar and often crowded curbside, other traffic moving, large group boarding at once; monitor lines students up, controls the flow at the door, verifies headcount against the roster, and manages equipment being carried aboard.

Disruptive or emergency boarding/exiting events: a student refuses to board or bolts toward the roadway, a shoving fight at the door, a rider becomes ill on the steps, or a roadside breakdown/evacuation drill requiring students to be directed out the front and rear doors to a safe assembly point away from traffic.

sources.system: CrossBot (Digital Twin Smart Robot crossing guard)
sources.developer: Hovannes Kulhandjian, Fresno State Transportation Institute / Mineta Transportation Institute
sources.title: CrossBOT for Safer Pedestrian Crossings - Fresno State Transportation Institute
sources.claim: CrossBot is a university research prototype 'crossing-guard robot' that uses lidar/cameras and AI to detect pedestrians and vehicles in a school zone and signal when it is safe to ...; it provides no physical assistance, no supervision of individual children, and is not a deployed product.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: guarding a child pedestrian crossing near a school. It is the closest robotic system found to directing children around traffic, but it only detects and alerts; it does not marshal students at a bus door, physically steady children on steps, operate a lift, intervene with a bolting child, or verify headcounts, so capability does not transfer to completing this task.

sources.title: LG Cloi GuideBot Enhances Customer Service at DFW
sources.claim: LG CLOi GuideBot is a commercially deployed autonomous service robot that navigates public terminals (e.g., DFW Airport Terminal D) and can escort adult travelers to destinations, but it only provides wayfinding and information — it does no physical handling of people and no safety supervision of children.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: guiding people through a structured facility. It shows autonomous people-guiding in an E2 setting, but the objects here are children whose safety depends on physical assistance, restraint from traffic, lift operation and behavioral control — none of which this platform performs, so it cannot complete the bus-boarding instance at worker quality.

tasks.label: Direct students evacuating the bus during safety drills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Required rear-emergency-door drill in the school bus loading zone/bus yard with a full load of elementary riders: monitor tells students to leave belongings and stay seated, moves down the narrow aisle, opens and holds the rear emergency door, climbs down, then physically steadies/lowers each child (semi-squat, jump-down) to the pavement, keeps the line moving, and leads them ~100 ft away before a head count.

Front service-door evacuation drill with mixed-age riders in a school parking lot: monitor gives verbal commands row by row, controls crowding on the stepwell, keeps students clear of the bus and passing vehicles, counts heads, and re-boards the group in order.

Drill on a special-needs bus: monitor releases safety harnesses/star-buckles, transfers or drags non-ambulatory students on an evacuation blanket toward the exit, coaches wheelchair riders and medically fragile students, calms students with autism or sensory sensitivities, and directs an aide/older student helpers.

Drill using alternate exits (side emergency door, roof hatch, kick-out windows) with middle/high-school riders in the bus yard: monitor demonstrates the latch, assigns and supervises two student helpers, spots students climbing out, and inspects that the bus is empty.

Pre-drill instruction and walkthrough on a parked bus or in a classroom: monitor explains evacuation rules, points out exits and latches, assigns seats/helpers, answers student questions, and signs the district drill documentation.

Practice or unplanned evacuation off-site — roadside shoulder on a field trip, gravel or grassy verge, live traffic, weather — where the monitor directs students out of the exit, keeps them off the roadway, and moves them to a safe assembly point.

sources.system: Robot-guided evacuation research platforms (survey of the field)
sources.developer: Alan R. Wagner, Penn State University (review in Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.date: 2021-07 (review; state of field unchanged for deployed systems as of 2026)
sources.title: Robot-Guided Evacuation as a Paradigm for Human-Robot Interaction Research
sources.claim: Robot-guided emergency evacuation of people remains a research paradigm studied in laboratory and simulated building settings; the literature proposes a roadmap toward future autonomous evacuation robots rather than reporting a fielded system that supervises and physically assists evacuees.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: guiding humans to exits during an emergency/drill. It is the closest robotic analogue to directing students off a bus, but it covers only route signalling in mapped buildings, with no boarding of a vehicle, no door operation, and no physical handling of children.

sources.title: Schools & Higher Education | Knightscope
sources.claim: Autonomous security robots are deployed on school and university campuses, but their function is patrolling, monitoring and recording traffic and pedestrians — they do not manage, instruct, or physically assist students.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous presence and monitoring on school premises. It shows what is actually deployable in the school environment today — sensing and recording only — and therefore does not transfer to directing and physically assisting children out of a bus.

sources.system: n/a (task-content reference for judging what completion requires)
sources.developer: Prince George's County Public Schools (Administrative Procedure 3541.35)
sources.title: Administrative Procedure 3541.35 - Evacuation of School Buses
sources.claim: District school-bus evacuation procedures require the adult assistant to stay at the emergency door controlling students as they leave, verify each student's posture before jumping down, and then sweep the bus to confirm everyone is out — a supervisory-plus-physical role.
sources.transferJustification: Not a robotic system: cited only to establish the accepted output of the instance (physical control of children at the exit plus a bus sweep), against which robotic evidence is measured.

tasks.label: Operate a wheelchair lift to load or unload wheelchairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Morning/afternoon home stop at a residential curb or driveway: monitor deploys the bus's hydraulic lift, backs the student's occupied manual or power wheelchair onto the platform, turns off chair power/sets wheel locks, closes the roll stop and applies the lift belt, raises the platform, pulls the occupied chair into the bus, positions it forward-facing over the floor anchors, attaches four tie-down straps and the lap/shoulder occupant restraint, and hands off to/receives from a parent. Student cannot self-propel.

School arrival/dismissal at the school's bus loading zone: same lift-and-secure procedure on a school-controlled paved apron or curb ramp, with several buses staged, staff present, and time pressure from the bell schedule; student in an occupied wheelchair who cannot self-propel.

Older student who is physically and cognitively able to drive their own power wheelchair on and off the lift platform: monitor operates the lift controls, guards the platform edges, then positions and secures the chair with four-point tie-downs and fastens the student's lap/shoulder belt inside the bus (typically at a school or program site).

Loading/unloading an unoccupied mobility device: the student transfers (or is transferred) to a bus seat and the empty wheelchair or adaptive stroller is rolled onto the lift platform, raised, brought aboard and secured/stowed so it cannot become a projectile; usually at a school or center loading area.

Adverse roadside conditions: rain, snow, ice or darkness; sloped driveway, gravel shoulder or broken curb; heavy power chair with occupant near the lift's rated capacity; agitated, medically fragile or seizure-prone student; occasional lift fault requiring the manual backup pump or hand crank to finish the cycle.

sources.system: Automated Transport and Retrieval System (ATRS) smart wheelchair
sources.developer: Freedom Sciences LLC / University of Pennsylvania (ICRA 2006 paper)
sources.title: Vision-based control of a smart wheelchair for the automated transport and retrieval system (ATRS) - IEEE Xplore
sources.claim: Research system (ATRS) in which a powered wheelchair autonomously drives onto and docks with a vehicle's rear lift platform under vision-based control, so the lift can load the unoccupied chair into a minivan/SUV.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: loading an unoccupied powered wheelchair onto a vehicle lift .... Same object class (wheelchair), same lift hardware and docking precision as the school-bus instance where an empty chair rides the lift, so performance transfers to that instance in a purpose-built vehicle/lift system.

sources.title: First Automatic Rear-Facing Wheelchair Securement Station Brought to Market : Q'STRAINT

sources.transferJustification: Related task: securing a wheelchair inside a bus, the second half of this task. instances.label: Monitor remains inside the bus during a short reverse maneuver in the school loading zone or bus lane; watches out the rear window/emergency door and calls out clearance and warnings to the driver until the maneuver is complete.

Rural or dead-end route turnaround: monitor exits the bus, walks to the rear, checks the path is clear of ditches, mailboxes, parked cars and pedestrians, and guides the driver with pre-agreed hand signals kept visible in the driver's mirror.

End-of-route parking in the district bus yard or school lot: monitor stands off the rear quarter and signals the driver into the assigned slot between other buses, watching for yard staff and adjacent mirrors.

Backing at or near a residential stop or tight cul-de-sac with students present: monitor positions to keep students clear of the path, scans for late-comers and small children, and signals stop/continue to the driver.
Field trip or activity run in an unfamiliar lot (stadium, museum, other school) at dusk or in rain/snow: monitor spots the reverse among pedestrians, parked vehicles and low-visibility conditions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-run walkthrough of the bus at the school loop or district yard: walk the 12–15 inch aisle checking each row, pick up wrappers, juice boxes, water bottles, papers and food waste from seats, floor and under seats, bag it, and set aside left-behind backpacks, jackets and phones for lost-and-found. Done after most runs.

End-of-day or weekly floor cleaning at the bus depot: sweeping or shop-vacuuming the ribbed rubber aisle floor, stepwell and under-seat areas of dirt, sand, road grit, crumbs and small debris on a fleet of standard buses parked in the yard/garage.

Wiping down interior surfaces with spray cleaner and cloth: passenger windows (smudges, handprints, condensation film), window sills, handrails, seat backs, stanchions, and the driver-area mirrors and dash, including periodic high-touch disinfecting.

Spot-cleaning a mess made during a run: spilled milk or soda soaked into a vinyl seat and floor, smeared food, tracked-in mud or snow slush, gum on a seat, or an occasional vomit/bodily-fluid incident requiring absorbent, disinfectant, scrubbing and bagging of contaminated waste.

Periodic deep clean of an assigned bus (end of term, or a special-needs bus): full interior pass covering trash in seat crevices and under seats, wheelchair securement tracks, harnesses and child safety seats, all windows, and a scrub of the whole floor.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: cleaning passenger seats in an aircraft cabin — rows of seats along a narrow aisle inside a vehicle, comparable surfaces (vinyl/fabric seats, trim) and comparable precision to wiping down school bus seat backs and interior surfaces.

sources.claim: Under an FTA SBIR award, Advent Innovations built Yogi-BOT, a robot that enters a transit bus and travels down the aisle applying liquid disinfectant and UV-C; it disinfects but is not shown collecting waste, vacuuming or wiping windows, and was still seeking pilot testing with transit agencies.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: picking up trash and vacuuming a passenger-vehicle cabin in a purpose-built depot bay. sources.title: Figure humanoid robot cleans cluttered living room in new video demo

sources.transferJustification: Related task: tidying loose objects and wiping surfaces in a room. It is the closest general-purpose litter-collection capability, but it is a staged room demo with open floor space; no demonstration exists of it boarding a vehicle or clearing waste from a narrow bus aisle and under-seat crevices.

sources.title: Roborock's $2,600 robot vacuum with a mechanical arm is an incredible flex with a weird price tag - Android Authority

Payload and object range are far below bus litter (bottles, backpacks, food waste), and the unit cannot board a bus or fit a 12-15 inch aisle, so it does not substantiate the bus instances.

tasks.label: Open and close school bus doors for students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood route stop: the bus halts at a residential curb, the monitor opens the front service door as it stops, watches 1-6 ambulatory K-12 students climb the steps or step down onto the sidewalk, checks the stairwell and danger zone (dropped items, backpack straps, a child turning back), and closes the door before the bus pulls away; repeated 20-40 times per run in rain, snow, glare and darkness.

School campus loading zone: at the bus loop at arrival or dismissal, the monitor opens the service door for a surge of 40-60 students, holds it open through several minutes of boarding/exiting, keeps the stairwell clear, and closes it only after the aisle and steps are clear and school staff signal.

Special-needs route with a wheelchair lift: at a home curb or an accessible school bay, the monitor opens the lift-side door(s) before the lift cycles, keeps the doorway clear while the platform raises and lowers with a student in a chair, then closes and latches the door after the student is aboard.

Yard/depot, pre-trip and post-trip: at the district bus yard the monitor opens the service door for boarding and the pre-trip walkthrough, cycles the door to confirm it operates and seals, and closes and secures all doors after the post-trip sweep at end of shift.

Emergency: during an evacuation drill or an actual incident at the roadside, the monitor releases and pushes open the rear (or side) emergency exit door, holds it while students exit and jump down, and re-secures it afterward.

Same class of act as opening/closing a bus service door for students - a powered passenger door, opened on arrival, held for boarding, and closed only after the threshold is verified clear, with obstruction detection and a no-move interlock. Setting is an institution-controlled station rather than a curbside.

sources.title: Come along for a ride in the Zoox robotaxi, an autonomous vehicle that could reinvent the way you move around the city

tasks.label: Apprehend shoplifters in accordance with guidelines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Big-box/discount store: plainclothes LP agent, having observed selection and concealment on the floor and via CCTV, approaches the subject just outside the last point of sale or in the vestibule, identifies self, and asks the subject to return; compliant subject is escorted through the sales floor to the LP office, merchandise is recovered, subject is held pending police or civil demand, report completed.

Mall apparel/specialty store: LP detective stops a subject at the storefront or in the mall common area, escorts them back to a small stockroom/office, recovers concealed goods from bags or clothing, keeps continuous observation of the detainee (who may be uncooperative, crying, or attempting to leave) until police arrive and take custody.

Non-compliant subject flees or pulls away at the stop: foot pursuit into the parking lot, sidewalk or street, physical control hold, takedown or handcuffing within use-of-force policy, control of a struggling person, and return of the subject to the store — weather, bystanders, traffic and unpredictable terrain all in play.

High-shrink urban grocery/drug store: aggressive subject or an organized retail crime crew pushing out a loaded cart; multi-agent team stop with weapons risk, de-escalation, judgment call on whether policy permits an apprehension at all (many such events end in break-off/observe-and-report), plus recovery of merchandise and evidence.

Subject stopped at the interior exit doors refuses to comply but does not run: agent positions to block egress, verbally holds the subject, radios for backup and police, maintains reasonable-force detention in front of customers, and transfers custody to responding officers with the recovered goods and a statement.

sources.title: Can robots help keep us safe? | National Geographic
sources.claim: Knightscope's K5 and related autonomous security robots patrol commercial properties autonomously but are explicitly not designed to police people or apprehend suspects; they act as sensors that summon humans.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task: autonomous security patrol and theft detection in retail and commercial settings. It does not transfer to apprehension because the source states the same systems are not built to detain or apprehend people.

sources.transferJustification: Related task is guard patrol/intervention; cited to show the capability boundary — no fielded security robot performs the physical stop, control and escort that apprehension requires.

sources.system: Knightscope K5 / K1 Autonomous Security Robots

sources.claim: Knightscope characterises its fielded robots' physical role as deterrence — conspicuous presence, lights and audio — not enforcement or detention.
sources.transferJustification: Developer's own description of the deployed system's physical role in loss-prevention settings; deterrence and patrol do not transfer to physically detaining and escorting a suspect.

sources.system: Autonomous ground security robots and security drones (industry class comparison)
sources.title: Security Guards vs. Robots vs. Drones: 2026 Cost and Performance Comparison
sources.claim: A 2026 comparison of guards, robots and drones for physical protection concludes robotic systems provide assessment but not physical intervention, and therefore carry no use-of-force or false-arrest exposure.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is on-site security response; cited to establish that as of 2026 no commercially fielded security robot performs the use-of-force physical intervention that shoplifter apprehension entails.

tasks.label: Verify proper functioning of physical security systems, such as closed-circuit televisions, alarms, sensor tag systems, or locks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine EAS / sensor-tag system check at a big-box or specialty store: LP specialist carries a live test tag through each entrance/exit pedestal at several speeds and heights, confirms the pedestal alarms and counts, checks pedestal alignment and interference, and tests POS deactivation pads and detachers with test tags; done with customers and staff moving through the doorway.

CCTV health check: LP specialist reviews the DVR/NVR or VMS at the office monitor bank to confirm every camera is live and recording with correct date/time, then walks the sales floor, stockroom and lot to confirm each camera is present, aimed at its intended field of view, unobstructed by signage or stock, dome clear of dust/haze, tests PTZ presets, and cleans or re-aims domes and flags failed cameras for service.

Intrusion/panic alarm test: LP specialist coordinates with the central monitoring station, arms/disarms the panel, trips door contacts on rear and emergency exits, walk-tests motion detectors and glass-break sensors, presses panic/duress buttons, verifies sirens and strobes sound and that each zone reports correctly to the monitoring company, then logs results.

Lock and physical barrier verification: LP specialist tries keys and codes on exterior and stockroom door locks, cylinder locks, padlocks on gates and trailers, safe/cash-office locks, jewelry and electronics showcase locks and security cages; checks latch engagement, strike alignment, closers and panic hardware, and reports sticking or failed hardware for repair.

Comprehensive multi-system security audit during a district visit or new-store/remodel turnover: LP specialist walks an unfamiliar store end-to-end, verifies all of the above systems plus signage, fitting-room controls, key control and safe procedures against a checklist, works around aging and non-standard equipment and varying layouts, documents findings and opens work orders with vendors.

sources.system: Kamtronix High Precision Door Lock Testing Machine
sources.title: High Precision Door Lock Testing Machine Guide
sources.claim: Commercially sold door-lock testing machines mount a lock in a fixture and run automated cycles that operate the lock and record its performance, i.e. machine verification that a lock functions to spec.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is bench verification of lock hardware rather than an in-store lock check; it transfers to the E1 counterfactual because the same objects (cylinders, latches, handles, electronic locks) are operated by machine and pass/fail on operational performance is reported automatically.

sources.developer: BHMA accredited testing laboratories (e.g., UL Solutions, Intertek)
sources.title: ANSI/BHMA Grade 1, 2, 3 Classification System for Door Hardware
sources.claim: Accredited door-hardware labs verify locks and exit devices by mounting them in representative fixtures and running machine-driven operating cycles, followed by operational checks.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is certification cycle testing of door hardware; it transfers because the physical act being verified (operating a lock and confirming it still latches and releases) is the same act an LP specialist performs on a store lock, here done with the workpiece fixtured.

sources.title: OptoFidelity FUSION - Functional Tester For Pre-Owned Smartphones
sources.claim: A commercial automated tester with robotic device handling verifies camera functioning, including image quality and defects in the camera sensor, lens and lens cover, and issues pass/fail results.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is functional grading of smartphone cameras; it transfers to verifying a CCTV camera because the verification is the same measurement — does the imager produce a correct, defect-free image under controlled targets — performed on a fixtured camera in a purpose-built station.

sources.title: Testing and Quality Control for RFID Tag and Label Production - Voyantic
sources.claim: An inline machine test station presents every RFID tag to reader electronics and measures RF detection performance, automatically passing or failing each tag at production speed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is inline RF tag testing; it transfers to the sensor-tag-system check because the physical loop verified is identical — a tag is presented into a reader/antenna field and detection is confirmed to spec — with the tag presented by the machine instead of walked through a pedestal.

sources.system: MATT (Multi-Axis Test Tool) test automation robot
sources.title: MATT the Smart Device Test Automation Robot
sources.claim: A commercial test-automation robot physically actuates device buttons, switches and knobs and validates the device's response, running unattended test cycles for days.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robotic functional testing of device inputs; it transfers to alarm-panel/keypad/panic-button verification because the same physical actuation of buttons and switches with automated confirmation of the resulting device output is required.

sources.system: Averna automated functional test systems / UniLine test platform
sources.title: Functional Testing Solutions for Manufacturing | Averna
sources.claim: Automated functional test cells built for production verify electronic hardware behaviour, including communications and real product behaviour, with automatic pass/fail traceability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is end-of-line functional test of electronic assemblies; it transfers to alarm-system verification at E1 because a fixtured panel/sensor set can be stimulated and its zone and communication outputs confirmed automatically, which is what the alarm test verifies.

sources.title: Cobalt security robot to protect your people and places
sources.claim: Autonomous indoor security robots patrol human work facilities on scheduled routes and perform facility and environmental checks, but their function is observation and anomaly detection, not functional testing of the site's cameras, alarms, tag pedestals or locks.
sources.transferJustification: Cited as the closest E2 system: it performs autonomous rounds in structured human facilities, which establishes navigation there, but no source shows it testing a pedestal with a tag, trying locks, or confirming camera image health.

sources.system: Spot with Autowalk and Spot Arm

sources.claim: Autonomous legged inspection robots run recorded inspection missions in industrial facilities, capture sensor readings at waypoints, and can now open doors with the arm during missions (beta).
sources.transferJustification: Related task is autonomous facility inspection rounds; cited to show the state of in-situ E2 robotic inspection — equipment observation and door traversal — which does not extend to functionally testing security systems (tag pedestal walk tests, alarm zone tests, lock operation checks).

tasks.label: Identify and report safety concerns to maintain a safe shopping and working environment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine presence on the sales floor of a supermarket, big-box or department store: spotting floor-level hazards as they appear — liquid spills, broken/dropped merchandise, produce debris, wet entryway, cartons or pallets left obstructing an aisle — and immediately alerting an associate/manager and logging the hazard in the store's safety system.

Back-of-house sweep of stockroom, receiving dock and compactor area: spills and debris on the floor, cartons/pallets blocking aisles or the emergency exit path, doors left open or unsecured, disorderly stacking; findings reported to the store manager and logged.

Observing and reporting unsafe acts and person-related safety concerns: an associate lifting improperly or standing on a shelf/ladder wrongly, someone riding a pallet jack, a child climbing a fixture, an intoxicated or aggressive individual, a customer medical event — judging severity, intervening/coaching and reporting.

Scheduled documented store-wide safety audit against a compliance checklist: fire extinguisher tags and clearance, sprinkler clearance, exit door function and signage, first-aid kit contents, ladder condition and storage, chemical labeling, electrical cords — written report with corrective actions and follow-up.

Follow-up on a hazard or incident reported by staff or a customer (broken glass, a fall, a damaged fixture): go to the location, assess and verify the condition, photograph it, arrange containment, and write and submit the incident/hazard report with cause detail.

Exterior sweep of the parking lot, cart corrals, fire lane and entrance: ice/snow, potholes and cracked curbs, burnt-out lighting, obstructed fire lane, damaged carts, loitering; reported to the store manager or facilities ticketing system.

sources.title: Badger Technologies and Stop & Shop Stores Upgrade Marty the Robot at 300+ Locations

It transfers to back-of-house retail hazard spotting because both are route-based visual detection of spills, debris and clutter in an indoor, institution-controlled facility, require no manipulation, and end in a logged report to a manager.

sources.title: Spot at Cargill | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Spot has been running routine inspection and visual safety checks in a Cargill processing plant since mid-2024 as part of a program toward autonomous plant monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: safety-check walkarounds of a processing facility. Same activity class as a back-of-house safety sweep — traverse a fixed route, visually detect abnormal/unsafe conditions, report them — in a comparably structured, institution-run indoor facility.

sources.claim: Badger's PatrolBot is a commercial autonomous patrol robot for stores, warehouses and offices that automatically verifies doors are secured, extinguishers/AEDs are properly stored, and floors ... hazards.

tasks.label: Conduct store audits to identify problem areas or procedural deficiencies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scored operational/compliance audit visit at a big-box or department store: the LP specialist works a written checklist covering cash office and safe controls, key control, refund/void/discount paperwork, receiving and vendor-door procedures, EAS tagging and fitting-room/bag-check controls, employee awareness; interviews the store manager, walks front and back of house, and documents findings with corrective actions and a score.

Sales-floor shelf and stock integrity audit: walk every aisle to verify on-shelf availability against system counts, spot-count high-shrink SKUs, check price/label accuracy and planogram compliance, flag misplaced items, plugs, and gaps; produce a discrepancy list for the store team. Store open, shoppers and carts present.

Premises security sweep at opening or after hours: walk the perimeter, stockroom, receiving dock, compactor area and parking lot to confirm exterior and stockroom doors are secured and not propped, emergency exits unblocked, no unauthorized persons present, lighting adequate; log anomalies.

Physical security systems audit: test emergency-exit door alarms and EAS pedestals with a live tag, verify each CCTV camera's field of view, focus and recording/retention against the coverage map, check locks, keys and safe function, review alarm panel user list, and write up repair/deficiency tickets.

Cash-handling and transaction audit: count register drawers and the safe, reconcile deposit bags and banking logs, pull refund/void/no-sale/discount documentation and verify it against the POS journal (signatures, IDs, approvals), note variances and procedural gaps.

Combined audit of a small-format site (convenience store, pharmacy, or specialty apparel): single visit covering narrow-aisle sales floor, cluttered back room, locked high-value/controlled cases, cash controls and daily paperwork, with only one or two employees on duty who must be interviewed.

instances.label: Routine opening/closing security walk-through of a single store's sales floor and perimeter: confirm front and rear doors secured, emergency exits alarmed and not blocked or propped, no one loitering or concealed in fitting rooms/aisles, EAS pedestals and camera domes physically intact, high-theft fixtures and locking displays undisturbed. Store may be occupied or empty.

Back-of-house check: stockroom, receiving area and loading dock, compactor/baler area, cash office and high-value merchandise cage, employee entrance. Verify dock doors down and locked, cage and cash office locked, no propped exit doors, no merchandise staged near exits, no unauthorized persons; area is cluttered with pallets, carts and cardboard.

Functional testing of security equipment: arm/disarm the burglar alarm and walk-test motion sensors and door contacts, run tagged merchandise through EAS pedestals to confirm they alarm, test panic/duress buttons and exit-door alarms, confirm signals received at the central monitoring station, check lock/key and safe integrity.

CCTV coverage and image-quality assessment: compare live camera views against the current floor layout, identify blind spots created by new displays, seasonal sets or planogram changes, check for obstructed/dirty/misaimed lenses and failed recording, and specify camera repositioning or additions.

District/regional LP specialist's comprehensive security risk audit of an unfamiliar store (new site, remodel, post-incident or scheduled audit): full walk of building, equipment and access points, judgment about exposure and control gaps, written findings with prioritized recommendations discussed with store management.

Exterior perimeter and parking-lot survey, typically at night: lighting outages and dark corners, fence/gate condition, exterior door hardware and roof-access points, dumpster/compactor area, cart corrals, loitering or staged vehicles in the store's own lot.

tasks.label: Respond to critical incidents, such as catastrophic events, violent weather, or civil disorders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Violent weather event (tornado warning, hurricane, severe thunderstorm, blizzard) hits an open big-box or mall store: the LP specialist activates the severe-weather plan, physically moves customers and associates away from glass and into an interior shelter area, closes and secures entrance doors and rolling grilles, kills exposed power/equipment, keeps people in place through the event amid noise, panic, possible water intrusion and debris.

Civil disorder, mass smash-and-grab or crowd surge at or near the store: specialist orders lockdown, physically closes/locks doors and drops security gates, moves associates to a back-of-house safe room, disengages from offenders, protects high-value merchandise where safe, and holds the perimeter until police arrive.

In-store emergency with the building otherwise intact and orderly: fire alarm activation, gas smell, power outage, or medical emergency. Specialist sweeps the sales floor and fitting rooms, guides customers out through designated exits, meets the fire department, retrieves the AED/first-aid kit, and confirms the store is clear before re-entry.

Post-event response at a damaged store: specialist enters after the storm/fire/riot, assesses structural and merchandise damage amid broken glass, standing water and downed fixtures, photographs and documents, arranges/assists boarding up broken storefront glass, secures the shell of the building overnight, and guards salvageable inventory.

Violent critical incident inside an intact store: armed robbery, active assailant, or hostile person. Specialist initiates lockdown or evacuation, moves people to cover, calls and briefs police, renders first aid to injured, preserves the scene, and manages witnesses.

Capability does not transfer to critical-incident response because the robot only senses and reports; it cannot shelter or evacuate people, lock down a storefront, render aid, or mitigate storm/riot damage.

tasks.label: Inspect supplies, equipment, or work areas to ensure conformance to established standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Receiving check at the back door of a restaurant/hotel kitchen: chef meets the produce, protein, dairy and dry-goods delivery, counts cases against the invoice, opens boxes, probes/feels temperature of chilled and frozen items, looks and smells for spoilage, bruising and off odors, checks pack dates and label integrity, rejects sub-standard cases and signs off.

Pre-service line check / walkthrough of stations in a busy restaurant kitchen: chef inspects each station for cleanliness and sanitizer buckets, verifies mise en place quantity and quality (tastes sauces, checks cuts and portions), takes hot- and cold-holding temperatures with a probe, checks covered and dated containers, and directs corrections before service.

Routine equipment condition round: chef walks the kitchen and walk-ins checking that refrigeration is holding temperature (reading thermometers and gauges), listening for failing compressors or mixer motors, spotting leaks, overheating or units not running, and reporting anomalies to maintenance.

Hands-on functional equipment checks: firing burners and pilot lights, verifying oven calibration with a thermometer, checking fryer oil quality with test strips, titrating dish-machine sanitizer, checking slicer blades, gaskets, knife edges and hood/grease filters, tagging out unsafe equipment.

Walk-in cooler, freezer and dry-storage inspection: chef opens and inspects prepped containers and part-used cases, checks date dots and FIFO rotation, smells and looks for spoilage, verifies covering and off-floor storage, and looks for leaks, ice build-up and pest signs, discarding non-conforming stock.

Closing / health-code readiness inspection of work areas in a restaurant, institutional cafeteria or hotel banquet kitchen: chef verifies surfaces and equipment were cleaned and sanitized, floors and drains clear, food correctly stored and labeled, chemicals segregated, hand sinks stocked, and completes the sanitation/HACCP log.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Independent full-service restaurant: produce distributor drops 5-10 mixed cases inside the back door or in a rear hallway. Chef counts cases and loose units against the invoice, opens boxes, checks lettuce/tomatoes/herbs for wilt, bruising, mold, ripeness and size, pulls bad units, marks credits and signs the invoice, then moves product to the walk-in.

Meat, seafood and dairy delivery at a restaurant kitchen: chef probes or IR-guns case temperatures, checks case weights on a receiving scale, inspects vacuum packs for leaks and bloom, smells and eyes whole fish/shellfish (gills, eyes, firmness, odor), verifies cut specs, lot codes and use-by dates, rejects temperature-abused or off product.

Broadline dry-goods delivery (canned goods, flour, oils, paper/disposables) wheeled in on a hand truck: chef counts cases and eaches against the invoice, checks for crushed, dented, leaking or infested cases, verifies SKUs and unauthorized substitutions, checks expiration dates, signs and files the paperwork.

Institutional/high-volume operation (hotel banquet kitchen, hospital, school district, casino) receiving at a loading dock: multiple palletized and refrigerated deliveries, formal HACCP receiving procedure with temperature logging, platform scale weighing of catch-weight items, pallet and case count verification against purchase order, damage/date checks.

Small or mobile operation and direct/artisan supply: food truck, small caf arm-to-table chef receiving at the curb, a farmers-market pickup, or an off-site catering event. Farmer or artisan hands over a heterogeneous mix (mixed herbs, eggs, live shellfish, cheeses, foraged items) in reused crates, in variable light and weather; chef eyeballs, smells and hand-counts everything.

Receiving inspection at the kitchen's back door: chef opens cases of produce, fish, meat, dairy and dry goods, checks temperature with a probe, looks/smells for spoilage, bruising, off-odor, cloudy fish eyes, checks pack dates, counts and grades against spec, and accepts or rejects the delivery.

Expediting at the pass: chef inspects each plated dish before it leaves — protein doneness and internal temperature, portion size, sauce placement, garnish, plate cleanliness, correct components for the ticket — and sends it out, wipes/corrects it, or refires it, all within seconds per plate.

High-volume institutional or commissary kitchen (hospital, school district, hotel banquet, catering commissary): head cook checks large cooked batches — probes internal temperatures, checks hot/cold holding temps, samples appearance, texture and doneness of each batch, and records results on HACCP logs, rejecting or reworking batches out of spec.

Scheduled spot checks of prep and storage: chef inspects cooks' mise en place for cut uniformity, freshness and correct execution, and walks the walk-in/freezer/dry store checking stock for spoilage, mold, freezer burn, proper labeling, dating and rotation, pulling anything substandard.

Off-site catering or private-event work: chef checks food quality on arrival at a client home, tented venue or event space after transport — holding temperature, condensation, appearance and doneness of transported dishes — in a setting with no standard kitchen layout or equipment.

sources.transferJustification: Related task = automated grading/sorting of raw produce. It is the same judgment a chef makes when inspecting a delivery or walk-in stock (spoilage, mold, discoloration, malformation) on the same objects, with a physical accept/reject action.

instances.label: Full-service restaurant or hotel restaurant dinner service: the chef works the sauté/grill/fish station, cooking à la carte orders from a varied menu — proteins seared or grilled to requested temperature, à-la-minute pan sauces, garnishes, composed plating — across many simultaneous tickets with modifications and allergy substitutions.

Pre-service scratch mise en place in a restaurant kitchen: breaking down whole chickens, filleting whole fish, trimming and tying roasts, varied produce knife cuts, making stocks, reductions and mother sauces seasoned to taste, doughs and pastry components.

Uniform portioning and cutting of proteins to spec for volume service: cutting steaks, chicken breasts or fish fillets from a uniform incoming product stream to fixed weights/thicknesses, trimming and panning them for the shift.

Batch cooking of standardized hot dishes and components in a commercial kitchen: soups, sauces, chili, braises, rice and grains, pasta, stir-fries, and fried items produced from prepped ingredients to a written recipe for the day's service.

Institutional volume cooking (hospital, college, corporate, senior-living cafeteria): producing hot entrées, bowls, pasta dishes and salads to a cycle menu and to order, plated or panned for cafeteria/steam-table service, using standard house ingredients and dietitian-approved recipes.

Cooking for functions and special guests: hotel/catering banquet production on deadline (large-batch roasting and braising, hot-holding, plating or panning hundreds of covers to a service time), and off-premise work in private homes, tents and food trucks for special guests.

instances.label: Restaurant kitchen, pre-service: executive chef gathers line cooks at a prep station and physically demonstrates a new hands-on technique (breaking down a whole fish, a new knife cut, a pan sear/pan sauce emulsification, a plating standard), narrating the cues, then watches each cook attempt it and corrects grip, timing, temperature and seasoning until they can reproduce it.

Any commercial kitchen: chef trains staff on a newly installed piece of equipment (combi oven, immersion circulator, vacuum sealer, blast chiller, high-speed oven, new slicer/mixer) — walks through controls and programs, safety interlocks and PPE, runs a live test batch, demonstrates breakdown and sanitation, and confirms each cook can operate it unsupervised.

High-volume institutional kitchen (hospital, school district, university, corporate dining, hotel banquet): head chef rolls out a standardized recipe or new production procedure to multiple cooks across shifts — demonstrates batch scaling, cook-chill/holding steps, HACCP temperature checks, allergen segregation and portion control on the actual production line.

Pre-service menu-launch demo for the whole brigade: chef cooks the new dishes in front of the team, explains ingredient sourcing, doneness and plating specs, has staff taste, answers questions, then has each station cook fire a practice ticket while the chef critiques against the spec plate.

Off-premise setting: chef demonstrates a technique at a catering event kitchen, food truck, pop-up, or outdoor festival station using portable/improvised equipment, unfamiliar layout, variable power/water, ambient conditions and a crew assembled for the event.

sources.title: Miso Robotics develops smaller, faster Flippy | Restaurant Dive

sources.transferJustification: Related task: cooking at a station in a commercial kitchen. It is the closest deployed capability in the same environment, and it shows current restaurant robotics is confined to a single dedicated, fixtured station with no capacity to demonstrate or teach a technique to staff.

sources.title: Breaking: Chef Robotics raises $43m Series A to scale AI-enabled robotics in meal assembly

sources.transferJustification: Related task: handling and portioning food at production scale. It demonstrates the ceiling of deployed food robotics — high-throughput repetition on a purpose-built line — with no demonstration, explanation, or coaching of human staff.

instances.label: Independent or chain restaurant: executive chef sits down with the sous chef and line cooks before service to plan a seasonal menu changeover, discussing which produce and fish are coming into season, which current dishes are underperforming, and what the kitchen's station layout and staffing can execute at peak covers. Output is a revised menu draft and dish concepts.

Hotel, banquet, or catering operation: chef collaborates with the catering sales manager and event planner on menus for a booked function, working from a guaranteed guest count, a per-head budget, dietary restriction lists, and the constraints of off-site or ballroom service. Output is an agreed banquet menu and per-guest costing.

Institutional foodservice (school district, hospital, university, corrections, corporate cafeteria): chef or head cook works with a registered dietitian, purchasing manager, and unit managers to build a multi-week cycle menu meeting nutrition standards, commodity availability, and forecast participation counts. Output is an approved cycle menu with production quantities.

Recipe development and standardization session: chef works with cooks or an R&D partner to refine a dish concept — adjusting ingredient ratios, yields, and plating — and to write it up as a standardized recipe card with portion sizes, allergen flags, and plate cost. Involves tasting and iteration alongside the written spec.

Daily or weekly specials planning: chef confers with produce/protein purveyors and the sous chef about what is available, priced well, or needs to be used up, plus the day's reservation count and weather, to set the day's specials. Output is a specials list communicated to the line and front of house.

instances.label: Quick-service restaurant shift supervisor trains a newly hired crew member on a station (fryer, grill, assembly line): explains the procedure and standards, shows the sequence, watches the trainee perform it during a live shift, and gives corrective feedback until the trainee meets speed and quality standards.

Full-service restaurant kitchen supervisor delivers a pre-shift or scheduled group session on sanitation and food safety — handwashing, cooler and holding temperatures, cross-contamination and allergen handling, cleaning/sanitizing chemical dilution, temperature log completion — using verbal instruction, a checklist or ServSafe materials, and questions from staff.

Institutional foodservice supervisor (school, hospital, corporate cafeteria, catering) trains serving staff on tray-line and steam-table procedures, portion control, garnishing, allergen/diet-order accuracy, and customer service scripts, then signs off on a competency checklist.

Supervisor conducts equipment and workplace safety training: safe use of slicer, mixer, fryer and knives, lockout/cleaning procedures, hot-oil handling, slip/burn/cut prevention, and chemical safety data sheets; includes a walkthrough demonstration and documentation of the training for compliance records.

In-the-moment coaching and retraining during service: supervisor notices an employee holding food out of temperature, plating off-standard, or skipping a glove change, and corrects the technique on the spot, re-explaining the standard and verifying the employee repeats it correctly.
