sources.claim: Zoo containment doors between exhibits and holding areas are moved by remote crank operators worked by the keeper from outside the enclosure; the animal then walks through on its own. There is no machine control of the shift decision or of the animal.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shifting zoo animals between exhibit and holding. It is the standard technology used for this exact task and it is human-cranked, so it cannot support an autonomous positive judgment.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: moving identified large animals between pens for breeding management. Transfer is limited: it works only for herd animals habituated to a one-way race in a purpose-built lane, and does not cover catching, crating, leading on a halter, or shifting solitary carnivores/primates, which dominate the zoo and equine instances.

sources.claim: A commercial fish grader moves live fish through ten outlet tracks into different destination tanks, with the outlet openings driven by electric linear actuators under automatic control from a counter that sizes the fish and computes the split; the associated pumps move live fish between tanks and pens.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: splitting and moving live fish between tanks in a hatchery. Objects (live finfish), gentleness requirement and the water-connected, purpose-built plumbing are comparable to moving stock fish between holding and breeding tanks in an ornamental fishroom, which is likewise a bulk, water-borne transfer rather than individual manipulation.

sources.system: Power Pet Kennel Series automatic guillotine kennel doors

sources.claim: Kennel automation available for dog runs consists of powered guillotine doors that are remotely controlled from a central location, run on timers, or are opened by the dog's own collar transmitter; no system selects a designated dog and relocates it to a designated run.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shifting dogs between connected kennel runs. The door is remotely cranked, timed, or pet-initiated, so the machine neither chooses nor moves a particular animal; it cannot substantiate autonomous completion of a directed dog transfer.

tasks.label: Adjust controls to regulate specified temperature and humidity of animal quarters, nurseries, or exhibit areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Zoo or public aquarium: keeper walks exhibit and off-exhibit holding areas (reptile house, rainforest dome, penguin/polar exhibit, aquarium galleries), reads temp/humidity gauges and life-support displays, and adjusts thermostats, misting/fogging systems, basking lamps and water-temperature setpoints to species-specific specifications.

Boarding kennel, doggie daycare or municipal animal shelter: caretaker sets and adjusts ward thermostats, ventilation/exhaust and dehumidification for kennel runs, cattery, isolation and whelping rooms, changing setpoints seasonally and after washdowns to keep rooms in the required 65-80F / moderate-RH band.

Laboratory animal facility (vivarium) with mouse/rat holding rooms: technician checks each room's temperature and relative humidity against the required setpoint band, adjusts room controls or logs an alarm/work order, and verifies conditions after HVAC upsets.

Nursery/neonatal work: hand-rearing puppies, kittens, chicks or reptile eggs in incubators, brooders and animal ICU units at a vet clinic, zoo nursery or breeding facility; setting and stepping down temperature, setting humidity, refilling humidity reservoirs, and repositioning heat lamps/heat mats.

In-home animal care (pet sitter, in-home boarder, private breeder residence): at a client's house taken as found, adjust terrarium heat/humidity controllers, aquarium heaters, brooder lamps, space heaters and the house thermostat so pet quarters stay in the specified range while owners are away.

sources.developer: Control Services / Uhl Company (InsideIQ alliance), using commercial BAS platforms

sources.system: Siemens Building Technologies APOGEE building management and control system (Emory Division of Animal Resources)

sources.system: Brinsea Ova-Easy Advance Series II cabinet incubator with Advance Humidity Pump
sources.title: Ova-Easy Advance Series II Incubator User Manual (Brinsea)
sources.claim: Commercial cabinet incubators/hatchers read humidity inside the chamber and drive a water pump to hold humidity at the set level automatically, alongside digital temperature control, from an external water bottle.
sources.transferJustification: Egg incubation/hatching is the nursery variant of this task: holding a small animal enclosure at a specified temperature and humidity by driving heaters and a humidifier from probe feedback, the same loop used for neonatal brooders and reptile egg boxes.

sources.title: Herpstat 4 | Reptile Heat, Light & Humidity Controller | Spyder Robotics
sources.claim: Multi-output reptile/vivarium controllers hold enclosures at target temperature by proportionally modulating heat sources and provide closed-loop humidity control with a humidity probe driving misting equipment; widely used on home enclosures, racks and incubators.

sources.title: Neptune Systems – Aquarium Controllers, Aquarium Monitoring, and Aquarium Automation
sources.claim: Aquarium controllers in hobbyist and professional installations automatically switch heaters and chillers from temperature probe feedback and shut down failed heaters, maintaining exhibit/tank water at specified temperature.

sources.system: ecobee smart thermostats with humidifier/dehumidifier accessory control
sources.title: Configuring Accessories with ecobee thermostats
sources.claim: Consumer smart thermostats installed in ordinary homes control a whole-house humidifier or dehumidifier to a user-specified humidity level in addition to temperature setpoints and schedules.

sources.system: Munters Trio / Munters ONE climate controllers and automation
sources.title: Controllers and automation | Munters
sources.claim: Farm climate controllers act as the control layer of animal-housing climate systems, driving sensors and actuators to regulate heating, cooling and humidity; the Trio/ONE controllers continuously adjust ventilation from temperature, humidity and CO2 readings, replacing manual adjustment.
sources.transferJustification: Livestock-house climate control is the same task on comparable animal quarters: hold a specified temperature/humidity in a room full of animals by modulating heaters, fans, inlets and foggers, which is what kennel, cattery and shelter ward HVAC requires.

sources.system: ViperTouch climate and production computer with control cabinet
sources.title: Poultry Controller | ViperTouch | Climate Control | Big Dutchman
sources.claim: Climate computers for animal houses control the entire house environment fully automatically, including physically actuated air inlets, fans, curtains and multiple heating zones, using room temperature and humidity sensors.

sources.title: Robotics for poultry farming: Challenges and opportunities - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: An autonomous rail-mounted robot patrols animal housing measuring temperature, humidity, air velocity and CO2 in three dimensions, providing the roving verification of climate conditions that caretakers do by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the checking half of the task (walking animal quarters to verify temperature/humidity against spec); it is a mobile robot operating over live animals in an animal-housing building, the same setting as zoo holding rooms and kennel wards.

tasks.label: Anesthetize and inoculate animals, according to instructions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Animal shelter/humane society intake: care staff give core vaccines (DHPP/FVRCP, bordetella, rabies per protocol) subcutaneously to incoming dogs and cats of every size and temperament, restraining each animal on a table or in ... kennel run, checking the record and dose per the veterinarian's written instructions.

Shelter/high-volume spay-neuter or veterinary support: caretaker draws up and gives pre-anesthetic sedative/induction injections (IM/SC) to dogs and cats under veterinary direction, then monitors the animal as it goes down and recovers.

Laboratory animal facility (vivarium): technician removes mice or rats from cages on a rack, restrains each by hand, and gives IP, SC or tail-vein injections of test article or vaccine per study protocol to dozens of animals per session, then records the dose.

Laboratory animal facility: inducing and maintaining rodent anesthesia (isoflurane induction chamber and nose cone, or injectable agents), checking depth by reflex, monitoring vitals during a procedure and through recovery.

Zoo/wildlife park: keeper assists the veterinarian in immobilizing hoofstock, carnivores or primates with a dart or pole syringe in a holding area or chute, or gives routine vaccines to birds, reptiles and small mammals of many species.
Aquarium, fish room or hatchery: aquarist anesthetizes fish in an MS-222 bath and gives intraperitoneal vaccine or antibiotic injections before returning them to the system.

sources.claim: Nova-Tech Engineering hatchery machines (PSP/MPSP, Hatchling Support System) automatically perform vaccination of live day-old birds together with beak/toe treatment and counting; they are in routine commercial hatchery use and halved labor for bird treatment at a Hendrix turkey hatchery.

sources.claim: Pharm Robotics' SureShot uses a FANUC arm and RFID identification to inject dairy cows held in a bumper restraint, but as of July 2025 the fully automated stack had achieved automated shots on a model cow rather than validated autonomous live-herd vaccination.

tasks.label: Install, maintain, and repair animal care facility equipment, such as infrared lights, feeding devices, and cages.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Animal shelter, boarding kennel or veterinary clinic: in-situ repair of cage and run hardware — resetting or replacing sprung latches and hinges, straightening bent bars, patching a chewed-through kennel door, re-securing a broken feed-bowl bracket or water-bowl clip, tightening loose panels — with animals and staff in the ward and no two failures alike.

Zoo or aquarium: maintaining habitat and holding-area equipment — replacing burned-out infrared/ceramic heat lamps and UV bulbs in guarded fixtures over enclosures, resetting or rewiring timers, servicing misters, tank heaters, pumps and filters, patching mesh — reaching over or entering enclosures, often on ladders and around water.

Laboratory animal facility (vivarium): routine servicing of caging hardware and drinking/feeding devices — processing cages, wire bar feeder hoppers and filter tops through the cage-wash line, emptying, refilling and re-capping water bottles, reassembling clean caging ready for use, in a standardized cage-wash suite.

Laboratory animal facility: fixing mechanical faults on caging and support equipment — a ventilated rack blower that has stopped, a leaking or blocked automatic-watering valve or manifold, a jammed cage-wash conveyor, a failed rack sensor — diagnosing the fault in place and replacing the part.

Barn, stable or large-animal boarding facility: repairing stall doors, gates and latches, patching a kicked stall wall, fixing automatic waterers and hose lines, replacing heat lamps in foaling/whelping stalls, servicing barn fans, mending paddock fencing — dusty, wet, uneven ground with animals nearby.

Installing new equipment: unpacking and bolting together a new bank of cages or kennel runs, assembling and mounting automatic feeders and gravity waterers, fitting brood-lamp fixtures and brackets, setting up tank hardware (heaters, filters, lights), then leveling, anchoring and connecting to power/water and testing.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine servicing of animal drinking bottles and cages rather than repair. It transfers to the 'maintain feeding devices and cages' portion of this task because the objects are exactly the animal-care equipment named (cages, feeder hoppers, water bottles) and the machine returns them serviced and reassembled ready for use; it does not cover fault diagnosis or repair.

tasks.label: Train animals to perform certain tasks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Boarding kennel, doggy daycare or animal shelter: staff run short reward-based sessions with kenneled dogs to teach/reinforce cue behaviors — sit, down, stay, recall, 'place'/settle, quiet-in-kennel — using treats and a marker word, in the dog's run or an indoor training room.

Same dog-care facilities, hands-on handling training: loose-leash walking in halls and yards, polite kennel entry/exit, jumping/greeting manners, taking treats gently, desensitizing dogs to collar grabs, muzzles, grooming restraint and nail handling, and socialization outings.

Zoo or aquarium: keeper/aquarist operant-conditioning sessions at mesh, pool edge or training wall — target and station training, shifting between enclosures, crate/kennel training, scale training, presenting a flipper/limb/ear for voluntary injection, blood draw or ultrasound, plus show and enrichment behaviors, with bridge and food reward, adapted to each individual animal.

Racing stable, boarding barn or riding/therapeutic program: grooms teach horses ground manners — leading, tying, standing for farrier and vet, accepting tack and bathing, loading into a trailer, lunging or ponying young horses on the track or in a round pen.

Laboratory animal facility: caretakers/technicians shape rodents or primates onto behavioral/cognitive tasks over days to weeks (nose-poke, lever, go/no-go odor or touchscreen discrimination), progressing animals through training stages with food/fluid reward.

Detection or working dog program kennel: staff run odor-imprinting and discrimination sessions (target odor recognition and trained final alert) on scent lineups/wheels in the training building, before dogs move to applied searches.

sources.title: SF SPCA Partners with Companion on an Innovative Approach to Training
sources.claim: CompanionPro, an autonomous computer-vision dog-training device with a treat launcher, taught shelter dogs basic obedience behaviors to high responsiveness, and the SF SPCA moved to install the devices in its shelter facilities.

tasks.label: Order, unload, and store feed and supplies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small kennel, boarding/grooming facility or vet-clinic animal ward: a delivery van drops 10-25 bags of kibble (20-40 lb), litter, bedding and cleaning chemicals at a back door or curb; the caretaker hand-carries or hand-trucks them through doorways and corridors into a supply room, stacks them on floor pallets and shelves, rotates older stock forward, and places the next order from a shelf count.

Animal shelter: a mix of ordered supplies and donated goods (opened and unopened food bags, cases of canned food, cleaning supplies, towels, toys) arrives in irregular boxes and sacks in vans and private cars; the caretaker unloads at the door, sorts usable from unusable items, and shelves them in a crowded storage closet or garage.

Zoo/aquarium commissary with a loading dock: a semi or box truck delivers palletized bulk grain, hay, pelleted feed and dry goods; the keeper/commissary worker moves pallets off the trailer with a pallet jack or forklift, checks them against the invoice, and puts them into pallet racking or a dry-storage bay.

Zoo/aquarium commissary non-palletized portion: loose cases of produce, frozen fish and meat boxes hand-unloaded from a delivery truck, broken down and stacked onto shelves inside walk-in coolers and freezers, with date rotation and cold-chain speed pressure.

Boarding/riding stable: a flatbed delivers 100-250 small square hay bales plus bagged grain into a dirt or gravel yard; the barn worker unloads bales by hand or elevator, stacks them in a loft or feed room, empties grain sacks into bins, and calls in the next hay/grain order.

Pet store / small aquarium retail stockroom: parcel and pallet deliveries of food, litter, tanks and accessories are received, unboxed, checked against the packing list, priced and shelved in a stockroom and on sales-floor shelves; reorders are placed from inventory counts.

sources.title: Warehouse Automation | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics Stretch autonomously unloads floor-loaded trailers and containers and builds palletized loads, handling cases up to 50 lb, in warehouse/distribution-center dock environments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unloading cases from trailers and stacking them onto pallets. It transfers to unloading/storing feed and supplies because the objects (30-50 lb cases/sacks of goods) and the lift-and-stack motion are comparable; it establishes capability at a dock inside a structured facility, not carrying goods into small storerooms.

sources.title: From case unloading to picking and beyond with DHL and Boston Dynamics - Automated Warehouse
sources.claim: DHL has commercially deployed Stretch robots for case unloading across multiple countries, at roughly 700 cases per hour, in its supply-chain warehouses.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (trailer case unloading); cited to establish that the deployment is real, commercial and in structured logistics facilities rather than a demonstration.

sources.system: Robotic bag palletizer / automatic bag depalletizer
sources.title: Automatic Depalletizer for 50 Lb. Bags of Powder Ingredients / Robotic Pallet Stacker for 50lb. Bags
sources.claim: Commercially installed robotic bag palletizers and depalletizers stack and unstack 50 lb bags of animal feed minerals and supplements (lift capacity to 110 lb) inside fenced automation cells, using 3D vision to locate bags and pallets.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unstacking/stacking 50 lb feed and mineral bags presented on pallets in a feed-processing plant. Objects (heavy floppy feed sacks), precision, and stacking pattern requirements match the 'unload and store feed' instance once the bags are presented as a purpose-built cell would present them.

sources.claim: Fox Robotics FoxBot autonomous forklifts unload palletized trailers at Walmart distribution-center docks under a multi-year deployment; the Mk3 loads and unloads single or double-stacked pallets autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: taking palletized freight off a delivery trailer at a dock. This is the same physical operation as the palletized-bulk-feed receiving instance (pallets of grain/feed moved from trailer into storage), with comparable loads and a dock-plus-racking layout.

sources.claim: Seegrid lift AMRs autonomously pick up pallets at inbound staging/receiving docks and transport them to bulk, floor or rack putaway locations in production customer facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: dock-to-storage pallet putaway inside a human-occupied facility. It covers the 'store' half of the palletized bulk-feed instance with the same payloads (pallets of bagged/cased goods) and the same indoor facility conditions.

sources.claim: Ambi Robotics' AmbiStack autonomously stacks unfamiliar mixed items onto pallets and into containers, and its integration with Pickle Robot's autonomous trailer-unloading system automates package flow from trailer to stacked pallet at Fortune 500 retail/logistics sites.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: handling heterogeneous, previously unseen parcels from an unloading point into stacked storage. It transfers to receiving mixed shelter donations/store stock only where the goods are presented to a fixed induction and stacking cell, i.e. at E1.

roles.title: Gambling Dealers
roles.description: Operate table games. Stand or sit behind table and operate games of chance by dispensing the appropriate number of cards or blocks to players, or operating other gambling equipment. Distribute winnings or collect players' money or chips. May compare the house's hand against players' hands.

tasks.label: Pay winnings or collect losing bets as established by the rules and procedures of a specific game.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Blackjack table on a casino floor: after each hand the dealer pays winners 1:1 (3:2 on blackjacks), takes losing wagers into the tray, and handles doubles, splits, insurance and side bets for up to seven betting spots, cutting and sizing chip stacks by eye at roughly 60-80 hands per hour with players' hands in the layout.

Carnival/specialty table games (Three Card Poker, Ultimate Texas Hold'em, Mississippi Stud, Pai Gow Poker): dealer settles several separate wager circles per player against a paytable (odds bets, bonus bets, pushes), pays from a chip tray and sweeps losers, keeping the game moving.

Roulette: after the ball drops the dealer marks the number, sweeps all losing colour chips off a crowded felt layout into the chipper/tray, computes multi-bet payouts (straight-up 35:1 down to even money) for several players and pushes stacks of colour chips to each winner, often with a Chipper Champ making the 20-chip stacks.

Baccarat / mini-baccarat: dealer pays winning Player/Banker/Tie and side bets, collects losing wagers from numbered betting boxes, tracks 5% commission markers per seat, at a fast pace with large-denomination chips and heavy surveillance scrutiny.

Craps: base dealer pays and takes bets across a busy layout for many simultaneous bettors (line bets, odds, place, come, proposition), sliding stacks accurately to distant betting boxes and sweeping losers, at very high speed and under boxman supervision.

Poker room: dealer awards the pot (and any side pots) to the winning player, takes the house rake and jackpot drop, collects blinds/antes and makes change, in a card room with players' stacks in front of them.

sources.title: CDK Chip Dispensing Kiosk | TCSJOHNHUXLEY
sources.claim: Commercially sold, self-service chip dispensing kiosk deployed on casino floors that verifies and dispenses physical casino chips of multiple denominations under machine control at over 3.5 chips per second.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: vending chips to a player rather than paying a game win. Transfer holds because the physical act is identical - counting out and delivering an exact value of casino chips to a player at a fixed station, with RFID verification - which is the delivery half of 'pay winnings' when the game is brought to a purpose-built machine.

sources.title: CRK Chip Redemption Kiosk | TCSJOHNHUXLEY
sources.claim: Commercially sold, self-service kiosk that physically accepts batches of casino chips from players, validates them with RFID and vision, and settles the transaction automatically.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: chip redemption rather than sweeping a losing bet. Transfer holds because the physical act - taking a batch of chips from a player, authenticating and accounting for them - is the collection half of 'collect losing bets' once the bet is presented at a purpose-built station.

sources.title: Chipper Champ 2 | TCSJOHNHUXLEY
sources.claim: Chip-handling machine used at live roulette tables in casinos for decades that autonomously sorts mixed colour chips and delivers them as neat stacks at up to 500 chips per ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sorting and stacking the chips a dealer has swept, not paying players. It shows machine handling of the exact objects of this task (roulette colour chips) at table speed and worker-grade accuracy once the chips are fed into the machine.

sources.title: Chip Dispensing Machine (CDM) datasheet
sources.claim: Automated chip vending machine deployed on casino floors as a 'satellite cage', accepting cash and dispensing casino chips in six denominations from hopper modules.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cash-to-chip vending. The mechanical capability demonstrated - hopper-fed dispensing of a specified number of chips of chosen denominations to a player - is the physical payout act required here when the game is presented at a machine station.

sources.title: Why Strip casinos continue to add electronic table games
sources.claim: Dealerless automated/electronic table games (e.g. Interblock roulette with a physical wheel plus player terminals) are widely deployed in Las Vegas casinos, resolving each round and settling wagers automatically without a human dealer, though winnings are credited electronically rather than paid in chips.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated settlement of table-game wagers. It substantiates that the rules-and-odds computation and per-player settlement of a table game runs unattended in casinos; it does not substantiate any physical chip movement, so it supports only the purpose-built-station (E1) counterfactual.

sources.title: Angel rapidly expanding smart table technology to more table games
sources.claim: State-of-the-art at-table automation on live casino tables is sensing only: smart-table camera/RFID systems identify bets, cards and hand movements and confirm that payouts are correct, while the human dealer still physically pays and collects the chips.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bet recognition and payout verification on live tables. Cited as the boundary of current live-table automation - no manipulator moves chips on a live layout - which is why the E2 (live casino floor) judgment is negative.

sources.system: Coin hopper payout mechanism in casino slot machines
sources.title: US6264556B1 - Gaming machine having note hopper/dispenser (Google Patents)
sources.claim: Purpose-built gambling machines have long paid winnings in physical tokens under machine control: hopper mechanisms in slot machines dispense the won coins into the payout tray after the machine determines the winning outcome.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: paying gambling winnings in tokens at a machine rather than chips at a felt table. Same act (machine determines the win under the game's rules and physically dispenses the correct number of tokens to the player) with comparable object size and counting precision.

tasks.label: Exchange paper currency for playing chips or coin money.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Blackjack/carnival-game table on a casino floor: a seated player drops $100–$1,000 in mixed bills on the layout mid-shoe. Dealer spreads and counts the bills for the surveillance camera, announces the amount to the floor supervisor, cuts and verifies the matching chips from the tray, pushes them to the player, then paddles the currency into the drop box.

Craps table, crowded and noisy: a player tosses cash on the layout ('change only'/buy-in). Dealer or stickman relays it to the boxman, the amount is called and confirmed, chips are cut and slid or placed at the player's position across a long table, and the currency is dropped.

Roulette table: player buys in with cash for non-value (color) chips. Dealer counts the currency, assigns an available color, dispenses the requested stack of color chips, sets the value marker on top of that color's stack in the wheelhead, and drops the cash.
Poker room cash game: player buys in at the table with cash; dealer/chip runner counts the bills, issues the corresponding stack of poker chips, and handles the currency per room procedure.

High-limit/baccarat room: large cash buy-in ($5,000–$50,000+ in banded $100s). Dealer counts and strapping-verifies large stacks with the floor supervisor and surveillance, cuts high-denomination chips, and the transaction is logged for MTL/CTR (ID and patron identification required).
Making change / coin or token exchange: breaking a large bill into smaller denominations or exchanging paper currency for coins or tokens for a player at the table or change point.

sources.claim: SuzoHapp's Chip Dispensing Machine (CDM) is ... commercial, self-service machine placed on the casino gaming floor that accepts banknotes (bunch note feeder, ~2,200-note stacker, counterfeit note detection) and dispenses casino chips in up to six configurable denominations, with transaction reporting and tamper/refill alerts.

sources.title: SuzoHapp chip dispensing machine receives global interest - GGRAsia
sources.claim: SuzoHapp's chip dispensing machines were put into live casino operation in Australia as a 'self-serve cage'/'satellite cage' on casino floors, exchanging money for chips without a cashier or dealer.

sources.claim: TCSJOHNHUXLEY's CDK Chip Dispensing Kiosk is a current commercial, fully automated self-service station on the casino floor that takes cash (13,000-note capacity banknote module) and dispenses chips at >3.5 chips/second, with RFID verification of dispensed chips, internal cameras/NVR audit trail, and AML transaction-limit controls.

sources.title: Chip Dispensing Kiosk - Butterfly Global Pte Ltd
sources.claim: A second supplier markets a chip dispensing kiosk for continuous casino-floor operation that accepts cash, validates/authenticates notes against counterfeits, and dispenses chips in multiple denominations integrated with the casino management system.

sources.title: MC720-DA - Standard Change-Makers
sources.claim: Standard Change-Makers manufactures bill-to-coin/token change machines that accept paper currency and automatically dispense coins or tokens; such changers are standard unattended equipment in casinos, arcades and other public venues.

tasks.label: Inspect cards and equipment to be used in games to ensure that they are in good condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Opening a blackjack/baccarat/carnival-game table in a casino pit: dealer breaks the seal on new decks (1-8 decks), spreads them face up in suit/rank order on the felt to confirm every card is present and the composition correct, scans backs for marks, bends, scratches or foreign cards, then washes and loads the shoe/shuffler, under pit and surveillance observation with a floor supervisor signing off.

Poker room deck handling: dealer inspects the deck at a deck change or table open (count, composition, no bent/scuffed/foreign cards), checks the pack coming out of the shuffler, and pulls and replaces individual damaged cards on player request during the session.

Mid-shift card condition check at a card table: dealer notices a bent, nicked, marked or stuck card during play (or the shuffler/shoe misreads a card), stops the hand, examines the card and the rest of the pack, and calls for a deck change or replacement card.

Craps: boxperson/dealer inspects dice before putting them in play or after a die leaves the table - visual check of faces, pips, logo and serial number, then micrometer, balancing caliper, set square and magnet checks for flats, floaters or loads; also checks stick, rails and layout.

Roulette (or Big Six): dealer/floor inspects the wheel and ball before opening - spins the rotor for wobble or noise, checks frets, pockets and ball track for damage, debris or tampering, checks the wheel head is level, and inspects the ball(s) for nicks, flat spots or metal inserts.

Other table equipment checks at open/close: card shoe and discard rack, shuffler condition and rollers, chip tray and chips (chipped, foreign or counterfeit), felt layout for tears/burns, dice cups, pai gow tiles, drop box and paddle; damaged items pulled and reported.

sources.title: Casino Card Deck Checker | TCSJOHNHUXLEY
sources.claim: A commercial, GLI-certified automated card verification machine deployed in casino back offices scans up to 8 decks (416 cards) in under a minute with two cameras, identifying missing, duplicate and misaligned cards and printing a verification report - the machine performs the deck inspection itself once decks are dropped into its input hopper.

sources.system: MD3 batch shuffler (Shuffle Master / Light & Wonder)
sources.date: 2023-04 product listing; machine in casino use through 2026
sources.title: Shufflemaster MD3 - Fully Refurbished - Innovative Product Suppliers
sources.claim: The MD3 batch shuffler, in wide casino use on blackjack and baccarat tables, uses card recognition to read and verify every card of up to eight decks as it shuffles, counting them and alerting the dealer to missing, added or swapped (unreadable/foreign) cards.

sources.title: DECK MATE 2 | Shuffle Machine for Poker Room
sources.claim: The DeckMate 2 poker shuffler performs onboard deck verification on every shuffle cycle: it checks the pack for incorrect quantity or composition, including missing, extra or swapped cards, and halts the game when the deck fails.

sources.title: WATCH: Hacker Shows Cheating Concerns With Poker Shuffler
sources.claim: Trade press confirms the DeckMate 2 is the standard, widely deployed shuffler in casino poker rooms, establishing that these card-verifying machines are in real operational use rather than one-off demonstrations.

tasks.label: Deal cards to house hands, and compare these with players' hands to determine winners, as in black jack.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Main-floor blackjack in a commercial or tribal casino: dealer pitches or shoe-deals two cards to each of 5-7 seated players and to the house (one up, one down), reads player hand signals, plays the house hand out under fixed house rules, then compares the house total against each player's hand to determine wins, losses and pushes, at roughly 60-100 hands per hour with money on the table.

Mini-baccarat or big-table baccarat on the casino floor: dealer draws cards from a shoe for the Player and Banker (house) hands, applies the drawing tableau for a third card, announces totals, and compares the two hands to determine the winner; crowded table, players may squeeze/handle cards in big baccarat, chips stacked in betting circles.

Carnival/novelty house-hand games on the casino floor (Three Card Poker, Ultimate Texas Hold'em, Caribbean Stud, Four Card Poker, Pai Gow Poker): hands are delivered from a single-deck shuffler or shoe, the dealer distributes them to each betting spot and to the house, exposes the dealer hand, checks the qualifier, and ranks the house hand against every player hand, including split/set rules in Pai Gow.

Live-dealer studio table serving online players (blackjack, baccarat, Dragon Tiger): dealer works a fixed, camera-covered table in a broadcast studio with no physical players or chips at the table, deals the house/banker hand on a timed cycle, cards are read by an optical shoe or overhead camera, and the outcome is compared and displayed to remote players.

Off-premises or non-standard venue work: charity casino night, corporate party or fundraiser in a rented ballroom, tent or private home, plus small cruise-ship or pop-up tables; portable folding layout, variable lighting and crowding, non-standard equipment, dealer hand-shuffles, deals the house hand and compares it with players' hands.

sources.title: Getting hands on with the future of live casino
sources.claim: CreedRoomz's ROBA robot croupier deals cards, collects them, reloads the shuffler and presents game outcomes, and has been running commercially in the company's live-casino studio on baccarat and Dragon Tiger — both games in which a house/banker hand is dealt and compared with the player hand to determine the winner.
sources.transferJustification: Baccarat/Dragon Tiger dealing is the same task class: the machine deals a banker (house) hand and a player hand from the same 52-card stock and the system compares them to determine the winner, as blackjack does.

sources.title: Soft2Bet elevates its Live Casino offering via a new distribution deal with CreedRoomz
sources.claim: ROBA is described by a commercial distribution partner as functioning as a real-life croupier in ..., providing automated 24/7 dealing, confirming it is a deployed product rather than a one-off demo.

sources.title: Robot plays blackjack dealer at Automate 2013
sources.claim: Yaskawa Motoman's dual-arm SDA10F ran a blackjack table for three players at a trade-show booth, using a MotoSight2D vision camera to read the face-up cards and playing the dealer's hand according to blackjack rules — i.e., dealing to the house hand and evaluating it against players' hands in a purpose-built setup.

sources.developer: Universität Hamburg, TAMS group (Fiedler, Güldenstein, Naß, Görner, Hendrich, Zhang)

sources.claim: A peer-reviewed, fully integrated robotic blackjack dealer deals cards to human players, visually detects which cards have been played, and recognises the knock/swipe hit-stand gestures players use, demonstrating the complete dealing-and-hand-evaluation loop autonomously in a laboratory table setup.

sources.title: SHUFFLE MASTER INC - Form 10-K - FY2011
sources.claim: Shuffle Master's casino-deployed utility machines physically deliver randomised hands of cards for the house-hand carnival games (Three Card Poker, Ultimate Texas Hold'em) and identify every card via optical card recognition, so hand composition is machine-known at live casino tables.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanically forming and delivering the dealt hands and optically identifying each card. It supplies the card-presentation and card-identification elements of dealing a house hand and comparing it with players' hands, on the exact games in this instance, though a human still distributes the hands.

sources.title: No Compromise – IAG (Inside Asian Gaming)
sources.claim: Angel's electronic reading shoe, the industry standard in Macau baccarat, reads each card's value automatically as it is drawn out onto the live gaming table, so a machine can establish the house and player hand values on a working casino floor.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated card identification during live dealing. It substantiates that the compare-hands/determine-winner element is machine-performed on a real casino floor, but the shoe performs no dealing motion, so it cannot complete the instance alone.

tasks.label: Stand behind a gaming table and deal the appropriate number of cards to each player.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Main-floor multi-deck blackjack in a commercial or tribal casino: dealer stands behind the table, takes cards from a shoe or continuous shuffler and pitches/slides two cards to each of up to seven occupied betting circles (skipping empty spots), then hit cards on request, amid chips, drinks, players' hands and pit surveillance, at 60-100+ rounds per hour.

Carnival/novelty table games (Three Card Poker, Ultimate Texas Hold'em, Let It Ride, Mississippi Stud, pai gow poker) on the casino floor: cards come out of an automatic shuffler in pre-set packets and the dealer distributes a fixed number (3-7) of cards face down to every wagered position plus the dealer/community hand.

Baccarat / mini-baccarat / Dragon Tiger in a casino: dealer draws cards from an eight-deck shoe and places two cards each on the Player and Banker card spots in the middle of the layout, adding a third card per fixed drawing rules; seated players wager but do not receive their own cards (mini-bac) or are passed the shoe hand (big bac).

Poker room Texas Hold'em/Omaha: dealer at a nine-handed table takes a shuffled deck from a shuffle machine and pitches two hole cards one at a time to each seated live player starting left of the button, then burns and spreads flop, turn and river, hand after hand for a 30-minute down.

Hand-pitched single/double-deck blackjack and high-limit/VIP tables: dealer hand-shuffles, pitches cards face down to players who pick them up and handle ..., deals to variable numbers of hands and spread bets, with heavy player interaction and card-security scrutiny.

Off-property dealing: casino-party/charity 'casino night' events or event-venue tables set up in a ballroom, tent or private room with borrowed layouts, uneven tables and unpredictable crowding; dealer deals blackjack or poker to whoever crowds around.

sources.title: Getting hands on with the future of live casino
sources.claim: CreedRoomz's Roba robotic croupier deals physical playing cards for live baccarat and Dragon Tiger tables in the company's live casino studio, taking cards, placing them on the layout, collecting them and reloading the shuffler; launched commercially in late 2022.

sources.title: Soft2Bet elevates its Live Casino offering via a new distribution deal with CreedRoomz
sources.claim: Roba runs unattended in CreedRoomz's live studio as an automated 24/7 dealing operation distributed to operators, indicating programmed autonomous operation rather than teleoperation.

sources.title: Two Hand ROBA Baccarat | CreedRoomz
sources.claim: CreedRoomz has extended the robot-dealt physical card portfolio to Dragon Tiger, Baccarat, No Commission ... a Two Hand Baccarat game run by two robot croupiers on one table.

sources.claim: A dual-arm industrial robot dealt blackjack to three human players on a card table at the Automate trade show, using 2D machine vision to read the cards and grippers to move them to each player position and play out the hand.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (dealing the appropriate number of playing cards to each seated player position) with the same objects and precision; the setting is a purpose-built demonstration table rather than a casino floor.

sources.claim: The card-handling automation actually deployed on casino floors is limited to shufflers and smart dealing shoes that shuffle, verify and present cards to the human dealer; the human still distributes the cards to the players.

tasks.label: Apply rule variations to card games such as poker, in which players bet on the value of their hands.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Casino poker room cash game: dealer pitches hole cards to up to nine seated players, applies the room's rule variations for the spread (no-limit vs limit betting, blinds/straddles/button rules, minimum raise, all-in and side-pot rules), reads boards, awards and splits pots of physical chips, drops rake, and rules on misdeals, exposed cards, string bets and out-of-turn action.

House-banked poker-derivative games in the casino pit (Three Card Poker, Ultimate Texas Hold'em, Caribbean Stud, Let It Ride): dealer deals fixed hands to up to seven betting spots plus the house hand, applies that game's posted rule variations and pay tables (e.g., dealer qualification, ante bonus, side bets), compares the house hand against each player's hand, and pays or collects chips.

Tournament poker at a casino/ballroom: dealer applies tournament rule variations (blind level changes, ante/big-blind ante, dead button, all-in betting rules, one-player-to-a-hand, chip races and color-ups, clock/floor calls), builds and splits side pots among all-in players, and pushes chip stacks.

Mixed and specialty poker games in a poker room: Seven-Card Stud, Razz, Omaha Hi-Lo, HORSE rotations, bomb pots, kill pots and promotional/jackpot rule variations; dealer must switch rule sets between hands, announce and explain variant rules to players, deal the correct street structure and split high-low pots.

Player-banked or card-room poker variants (Pai Gow Poker, California card-room games with collection fees, player-banker rotation): dealer sets the house-way hands, applies bank rotation and commission/collection rule variations, and settles each spot against the banker's hand with physical chips.

Off-premises charity poker night or casino-party event in a rented hall, club room or private residence: dealer sets up a portable table, explains and applies the host's rule variations to novice players, deals hold'em or a home-style variant, manages chips, and resolves rule questions informally.

instances.label: Opening a blackjack or carnival-game table at shift start on a casino floor: unlock and remove the float cover, break down and count the chip tray by denomination in stacks with the floorperson witnessing, verify the count against the opening table inventory slip, sign it and place it in the drop box, verify/spread a fresh deck or load the shuffler, set out cards and layout accessories, and signal the table open to players.

Closing a card table at end of shift or when the pit closes: count down the chip float by denomination with the supervisor, complete and sign the closing table inventory slip, deposit paperwork in the drop box, secure discards/decks into the card cabinet or box, arrange chips in the rack, and lock the clear float cover onto the tray.

Opening/closing a roulette table: verify each of the color (non-value) chip sets is complete (e.g., 300 chips per color across up to 8 colors) plus the value-chip float, count against the inventory slip with the supervisor, check the wheel, ball and marker, clear the chipper, then cover and lock float and wheel at close.

Opening/closing a craps table with a boxperson and crew: count a large multi-denomination bank including high-denomination chips, verify against the opener/closer slip, inspect and log the dice sticks and bowl, distribute chips into the rails, and secure the bank and dice under a locked cover at close.

Poker-room or small card-room table start-up and shut-down: draw a chip rack/dealer bank from the cage, count and verify it with the cage cashier or supervisor, set the table with cards, button and shuffler, and at close count the rack down, reconcile it, and return it to the cage.

Mid-shift opening or closing of an extra table (or a high-limit room table) in response to demand: quickly count and verify the fill/float including plaques or high-denomination chips with the floor supervisor while patrons are waiting at the table, sign the slip and open or shut the game.

instances.label: Poker-room prop/shill: sits in a live no-limit hold'em or Omaha cash game on the casino poker-room floor for a full shift to start and keep a short-handed game going — posts blinds, protects and peeks at hole cards, sizes and pushes chip bets, calls/raises/folds in turn without slowing the game, mucks at showdown, rebuys, and interacts with 5-8 human players and the dealer.

House shill at a blackjack, mini-baccarat or carnival card game in the pit: places a flat chip bet in the betting circle each round, receives face-up cards, gives hit/stand hand signals, splits/doubles by placing additional chips, and collects or surrenders chips, keeping the table 'open' until real players sit down.

House player at a pai gow poker or pai gow tiles table (games that need bodies to run): places the bet, receives seven cards or four tiles, sets them into the correct high and low hands face down within house rules, exposes at showdown, and settles the bet.

Shill at a craps table: buys in, places pass line/come/place bets with chips across a busy layout at the correct spots and correct times, calls bets verbally to the stickman over noise, and takes the dice and shoots when the dice come around (throw must reach the back wall).

Shill placing chips on a marked layout at roulette or sic bo: puts one or more chips on numbers, splits or outside boxes before 'no more bets', retrieves winnings, and repeats each spin to give the table visible action.

instances.label: Sports book counter: a patron hands a winning sports wager ticket across the counter; the writer scans/validates it in the book's computer system, confirms the ticket is unpaid and correctly graded, brands it paid, counts out the cash payout (typically $20-$1,000) from the drawer and hands it over, under camera and internal-control rules.

Race book / pari-mutuel window in a casino or racetrack: cashing winning mutuel tickets and vouchers (including prior-day tickets), paying refunds when an entry is scratched, and handling voucher balances and change due, at a teller window during simulcast racing.

Keno lounge counter: keno writer verifies a winning keno ticket against the drawn numbers in the keno system, pays the win in cash or credit, or applies the win to replay the same ticket for the next game(s).

Payoffs delivered on the floor: keno runner circulating a coffee shop, bar or lounge who collects tickets and carries winnings back to seated patrons; bingo floor clerk who responds to a 'bingo' call, verifies the card/serial against the called numbers, and pays the session prize in cash at the player's seat or the podium.

Large or reportable payoff at the counter: payout at or above IRS/Title 31 thresholds (e.g., pari-mutuel 300-1 and $600+ requiring a W-2G, withholding on $5,000+, $10,000+ cash requiring supervisory approval and currency transaction reporting) - the writer verifies patron identity, completes tax paperwork, gets supervisor sign-off and pays in cash or by check.

Moving a bet as house rules require: applying the value of a winning ticket or voucher directly to a new wager, voiding and reissuing a mis-written ticket, or moving/refunding a wager when an entry is scratched or an event is postponed, done at the writer's terminal with the patron's ticket in hand.

instances.label: Casino keno lounge: worker runs the game cycle — opens and closes the wagering window, operates the ball blower or random-number equipment, watches the 20-number draw, announces/posts the numbers, and verifies and pays presented tickets while enforcing house rules (no late tickets, correct ticket copies).

Live card game at a casino table (blackjack, mini-baccarat, pai gow): shuffle or load the shoe, deal to each spot, settle wagers in chips, protect the deck and enforce play rules, hand-signal decisions, and handle buy-ins and colour-ups at a normal casino pace.

Off-site or small-venue game conduct: charitable casino night, fraternal club, cruise or mobile casino party in a rented hall — tables and blowers set up ad hoc, layout differs each event, mixed-quality equipment, and largely inexperienced players who need the rules explained and enforced.

Big Six / money wheel or similar vertical prize wheel at a small table: players place chips on symbols, the operator spins the wheel, calls the winning wedge, collects losing bets and pays winners.

In-game irregularity and integrity handling at the wheel: ball spun the wrong way or failing to complete the required revolutions ('no spin'), ball leaving the wheel or coming to rest on a chip or debris, disputed late bets, periodic ball changes and inspection of ball and wheel head, escalating to a supervisor.

tasks.label: Compare the house hand with players' hands to determine the winner.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Blackjack-style round at a casino table: after the hole card is exposed, the worker reads the dealer's total against each player's already-visible total (including busts, pushes, naturals, split and doubled hands) and determines win/lose/push for each spot before the bets are resolved.

Baccarat/mini-baccarat: with both the player and banker hands exposed, the worker evaluates the two totals under the drawing rules and calls which hand wins or whether it is a tie, plus resolution of pair/tie side bets.

Pai gow poker or Asia poker: the house hand has been set per house way; the worker compares the house's high and low hands to each patron's corresponding hands, applying copies-to-the-house and ranking rules, and determines win, loss, or push for each seat.

Carnival card games (three card poker, Ultimate Texas Hold'em, Mississippi Stud, casino war): the worker determines whether the dealer's hand qualifies and compares hand rankings to each player's hand to determine outcomes for ante, play, and bonus wagers.

Irregular or contested comparison: a patron mis-set hand, an ambiguous or ranking-edge holding, an unusual payout ruling, or a patron dispute where the worker's determination must be reconciled with house rules and a floor supervisor before the winner is declared.

tasks.label: Monitor operations to ensure that standards for sound and image projection quality are met.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex screen checks during running shows: the projectionist walks auditorium to auditorium mid-feature, watching the screen for framing/masking errors, soft focus, dim or failing light output, color or 3D ghosting problems, and listening for correct fader level, missing surround channels, or distortion; deviations are noted for correction or reported to management.

Booth or office monitoring of the theatre management system across 8-20 digital screens: watching playback status, automation cue faults, ingest/KDM alarms, projector error codes, lamp hours and light-output warnings, and confirming each show is running to spec.

Responding to a mid-show quality report from an usher, manager, or patron ('sound too low', 'picture looks soft/dark'): entering the house, watching and listening from the seating area, and judging whether the presentation is genuinely out of standard or acceptable.

Scheduled technical quality control before shows or off-hours: projecting test patterns, taking screen luminance readings at center and corners with a light meter, running pink-noise/SPL checks per channel, and verifying results against SMPTE/DCI presentation standards.

Repertory, art-house, or specialty large-format venue running 35mm/70mm film: the projectionist stands at the port glass through the reel watching for scratches, frame jump, focus drift, and changeover cues while listening to the analog/optical sound track.

tasks.label: Start projectors and open shutters to project images onto screens.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Chain multiplex auditorium: at each scheduled showtime the operator (booth/manager) must bring the auditorium's digital cinema projector out of standby, start the show playlist, and get light on the screen — lamp/light source on, douser (shutter) open, correct lens/masking macro — for a dozen-plus staggered showtimes a day in a standard projection booth.

Independent, art-house or single-screen cinema: one or a few digital projectors, sometimes older or mixed-vendor equipment; the operator starts each show at showtime from the projector touch panel or a small TMS, occasionally after a live intro, and opens the shutter to put the image on screen.

Premium large format auditorium (IMAX digital/laser, Dolby Cinema, other PLF): show start at showtime under the PLF vendor's own show system, with intermissions/PLF-specific pre-show sequences, higher presentation standards and tighter timing.

Repertory/archival film show in a cinema or museum theatre: 35 mm or 70 mm reel-to-reel or platter presentation; at showtime run up the projector motor, strike/uncover the xenon lamp, open the douser to put the image on screen, and (reel-to-reel) repeat at each changeover.

Mobile/outdoor or temporary-venue screening: pop-up park, parking-lot or rooftop event, festival in a non-cinema space, projector and screen trucked in and set up on the day; at showtime start the projector and open the shutter with the crowd already seated, in ambient light/weather.

tasks.label: Open and close facilities according to rules and schedules.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Morning opening of a suburban multiplex: arrive at the scheduled time, unlock the staff entrance with a key/fob, disarm the intrusion alarm panel, switch on lobby, corridor and auditorium lighting, HVAC and marquee, unlock auditorium and restroom doors and the front doors at the posted open time, then power up projectors, media servers, sound processors and check each screen is ready before first show.

Nightly closing of a multiplex after the last show: shut down projection and sound equipment, walk each auditorium and restroom to confirm no patron is left inside and note hazards or lost property, close masking/curtains, turn off house and lobby lighting and set back HVAC, secure the booth, check and lock all exit and front doors, arm the alarm and complete the closing log.

Open/close of a small single-screen, arthouse or historic theater: physical key locks on multiple doors, breaker panels and manual dimmers, older projection gear (xenon lamp warm-up/cool-down or film platter) plus marquee and box-office shutters; the projectionist is often the only person on site and follows a written opening/closing checklist.

Booth-only open/close at a chain venue where managers and floor staff handle the building: at the scheduled times bring projectors, servers, sound and automation systems up before the first show and power them down after the last, confirming schedule, ingest and lamp/laser state.

Non-standard schedule opening/closing: early private or corporate screening, festival day, all-night marathon, or an early close due to cancelled shows or weather; unlocking secondary entrances, adjusting equipment power and lighting to a changed schedule, and locking up at an unusual hour.

tasks.label: Operate equipment to show films in a number of theaters simultaneously.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: First-run digital multiplex (8-24 screens): the projectionist/booth manager runs the day's shows across every auditorium from a central theatre-management console in the booth or manager's office - staggered start times, preshow ads, trailers, feature, plus automation cues that dim house lights, open masking/curtains, set the sound processor and douse/undouse the projectors; shows overlap all day and the operator watches the status of all screens at once.

Digital multiplex content operations tied to running simultaneous shows: receiving DCPs (courier hard drive, satellite or network), ingesting them, loading and validating KDMs, building or templating show playlists for each auditorium, then scheduling and launching those shows on many screens at once for the weekly program change.

Small independent / community / dine-in theater with 2-6 digital screens and mixed-vintage equipment: one person starts each auditorium's show (sometimes at the server touchpanel in each booth), keeps overlapping showtimes on schedule, and handles mid-show faults (audio dropout, wrong masking/aspect, server alert, projector fault) while the other screens keep running.

Repertory, archival or premium-format house running photochemical film (35mm/70mm) on one or two screens simultaneously with digital screens: film built on platters or large reels, projectors pre-threaded, shows started and run with cue-detection automation and interlocks, operator watching framing/focus and ready for breaks or brainwraps.

Non-standard venues: film festival or conference with several temporary screening rooms, a museum/university venue with mixed formats, or a multi-field drive-in - ad-hoc or seasonal setups, schedules shifting for Q&As and late content deliveries, several rooms projecting at the same time.

tasks.label: Perform regular maintenance tasks, such as rotating or replacing xenon bulbs, cleaning projectors and lenses, lubricating machinery, and keeping electrical contacts clean and tight.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex projection booth: rotate or replace the xenon bulb in a digital cinema lamphouse — power down and cool, don face shield and gloves, open the lamphouse, loosen anode/cathode clamp bolts, extract the pressurized quartz bulb in its cage, install and torque the new lamp, align it to the reflector, reset the lamp hour timer, verify screen light output.

Cleaning the optics of a digital cinema projector: projection lens elements, port glass, integrator rod and prism/DMD region — blowing dust, using lens tissue and optical solvent with care to avoid scratching or leaving residue, then checking the projected image for artifacts.

Routine housekeeping on the projector and light source: unscrewing access panels, vacuuming/blowing dust out of the cabinet and heat exchanger, washing or replacing air/dust filters, cleaning fan grills and exhaust ducting, and reinstalling panels — on a mounted projector in a cramped, hot booth.

Electrical upkeep: inspecting and cleaning lamp electrode terminals and connector contacts for oxidation/pitting, re-torquing terminal and busbar fasteners, checking ground straps, cable strain relief and rectifier/power-supply connections in the lamp power supply and projector cabinet.

Legacy 35mm/70mm film equipment in a repertory or art-house house: oiling and greasing intermittent movements, gears, platter/tower bearings and drive chains per the lubrication chart, cleaning the film path, gate and rollers of emulsion buildup, and checking sound-head and reel-arm mechanisms.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated device teardown. tasks.label: Set up and adjust picture projectors and screens to achieve proper size, illumination, and focus of images, and proper volume and tone of sound.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex digital auditorium, routine pre-show setup for a scheduled show: bring up the light source, select/recall the lens preset and masking for flat vs. scope, confirm image size, focus and framing on the screen, confirm light level, and set the fader level and audio format. Repeated many times a day across 8-20 screens.

Spot check / corrective adjustment during the operating day in a multiplex auditorium: image looks soft or geometry is off, brightness has drifted, or a patron complains the sound is too loud or too dull; the operator watches from the house and corrects lens focus/zoom, light output, and fader/EQ from the touch panel, booth, or TMS.

New auditorium install or periodic (quarterly/annual) recalibration: physically aim and boresight the projector, set masking travel limits and screen edges, measure light output at the screen with a photometer to hit 14 fL, set color/white point, and align the sound B-chain by placing measurement microphones in the house and setting per-channel level and EQ.

35mm/70mm film screening at a repertory house, festival, or archive: mount reels or build the platter, lace the projector, install the correct aperture plate and lens for the aspect ratio, rack framing and focus during the run, and set the analog/optical sound level and tone.

Mobile/pop-up event projection in an unstructured venue (park lawn, school gym, backyard, hotel ballroom): erect or inflate the screen, place and aim the projector at the right throw, set size/focus/keystone, and set up and level speakers or an FM transmitter before the audience arrives.

Permanent outdoor venue with fixed screen and booth (drive-in or municipal open-air theater): start up the digital projector for the evening's shows, set image size/masking for the format, set brightness appropriate to fading ambient light, and set audio levels for the FM/speaker feed.

tasks.label: Inspect projection equipment prior to operation to ensure proper working order.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex digital booth, pre-opening round: projectionist/manager walks a booth serving 8-20 auditoriums, powers up or wakes each digital cinema projector and server, checks touch-panel status and error/warning logs, laser/lamp hours and light output readings, cooling airflow and air-filter condition, and wipes lens/port glass before the day's shows.

Auditorium-side presentation check: run a test pattern or the pre-show trailer in each house and verify projected image (focus, framing, masking, brightness/uniformity, no dead pixels or debris shadows) plus sound (all channels present, correct level, sync), and, in 3D houses, the polarizer/silver-screen setup.

Repertory/art-house booth: inspect an incoming 35mm or 16mm print reel by reel on a rewind bench or inspection table before the screening - check every splice, torn or damaged perforations, tears, tape, curl, dirt - and flag or mark defects.

Film projector pre-show mechanical/optical inspection: check gate, aperture plate, sprockets, rollers, intermittent movement, tension, lamp house and lamp alignment, douser, sound head/exciter or reader, platter or reel arms, and run a short test loop for steadiness and sound.

Premium large-format house (IMAX with Laser, Dolby Cinema, 4DX): pre-show system check of the projection head(s), laser light source and cooling/chiller status, alignment/convergence test patterns, immersive sound channel check, and integration/automation status.

Drive-in, outdoor screening, or mobile/event projection: check trailer- or cart-mounted projector, cabling, generator/power, FM transmitter or PA, screen surface and rigging, and weather protection at a site whose layout and gear vary from job to job.

sources.system: Radiant Vision Systems ProMetric imaging colorimeters + TrueTest Automated Visual Inspection
sources.date: 2020 (product pages; systems in production use through 2026)
sources.title: Display Test - Application | Radiant Vision Systems

tasks.label: Perform minor repairs, such as replacing worn sprockets, or notify maintenance personnel of the need for major repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex projection booth: routine minor service on a digital cinema projector between shows — replace/clean intake air filters, clean lens and prism optics, rotate or replace a xenon bulb in the lamphouse (unbolt electrode terminals, torque, re-align), swap a failed cooling fan, reseat cards and cables; then run a test clip to confirm image and sound before the next screening. Cramped booth, hand tools, live-schedule time pressure.

A fault appears (no image, error code on the projector's touch panel, dropout in one audio channel, dimming light source, rattling noise). The projectionist walks the booth, inspects the projector/media server/sound rack, makes a trivial fix if it is one, otherwise localizes the fault, judges it beyond minor repair, and notifies the chief projectionist/service vendor with a description and ticket/log entry.

Minor repairs to sound and auxiliary equipment in the booth or amplifier rack: replace a blown fuse or failed amplifier module, re-terminate or replace a speaker/network cable, swap a media block or automation relay board, replace batteries/emitters in the 3D or assistive-listening system, then verify with test tones.

Repertory/arthouse 35mm or 16mm booth: mechanical minor repair on a film projector — replace a worn sprocket, rollers, pad rollers, or drive belt; adjust tension and lateral guide; lubricate the movement; splice damaged film — then thread and run test footage to check registration and steadiness.

In-situ fixes outside the booth on installed hardware: ladder work in the auditorium to re-tighten or re-aim a ceiling projector mount or speaker bracket, clean port glass from the house side, free a jammed screen-masking motor or limit switch, replace a burnt-out sconce/aisle fixture tied to the show automation. Seats, rakes, and darkness constrain access.

Drive-in, outdoor screening, or mobile/event projection: on-site troubleshooting and minor repair with the rig set up in a trailer, tent, or temporary booth — overheating projector, damaged run of cable, failing generator feed, loose lens mount — under weather and dust, with improvised fixes and a call to the equipment owner or vendor if it is major.

It matches the core of 'replace a worn sprocket/lamp/fan module' at E1 — the workpiece is brought to a purpose-built station and fixtured, fasteners are removed and re-torqued, the worn unit is removed, a fresh one installed, and the result is verified by an automatic health check before release.

tasks.label: Set up and inspect curtain and screen controls.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine pre-show/periodic functional check in a multiplex auditorium: from the wall panel or by firing the automation cue, cycle the curtain open/close and drive the masking between flat and scope, watch that travel completes to the correct stops against the projected test pattern, listen for binding or motor noise, and note screen/curtain surface condition. Dark, empty, seated auditorium between shows.

Setting and storing curtain/masking preset positions on the motor control panel: after a format change or service, jog top and side masking motors and the curtain until edges line up with the projected image, store each stop, then cycle through the presets to confirm they repeat.

Programming or editing curtain and masking cues in the theatre automation/TMS playlists for the week's programs (curtain open, masking change, close), then running a test playback in the auditorium to confirm each cue fires at the right point in ... show.

Correcting hardware when a check fails: resetting a tripped curtain controller, adjusting a motor limit switch or re-tensioning a cable behind or above the screen from a ladder, freeing a snagged curtain track, then re-running the cycle to confirm the fix.

Premium-large-format, single-screen or live-event venue setup: configure screen raise/lower, house drapes, curtain and masking presets for a nonstandard program (festival, live broadcast, 4DX/PLF), coordinate with stage and house-lighting cues, and verify by a cue rehearsal.

New installation or reconfiguration: mount and wire masking motors and the curtain controller into the automation contacts, set travel limits, commission the whole control chain and inspect it end to end before handover.

instances.label: Routine commercial multiplex show: the booth operator builds/runs the show playlist for each auditorium — pre-show music and ad reel, trailers, feature — and coordinates it with equipment operation: projector start, dowser, sound format and level changes, non-sync music fade, house-light dimming, tab curtain and screen masking moves. Many auditoriums, many shows per day, fixed booth and auditorium layout.

Special event at a cinema: premiere, festival screening, sing-along or Q&A. A live host speaks on a microphone over a music bed; the operator rides mic and music levels, kills the music, dims lights and starts the feature on a cue taken from the live speaker; occasionally a live musician accompanies a silent film and the operator must match the presentation to the performer.

Event cinema / alternative content: live satellite or streamed opera, concert, sports or church service. House music and slides before the feed, switch to the live input at the scheduled time, handle intermission audio and any local commentary, then post-event content — timing partly driven by the live feed's pacing.

Non-theatrical institutional venue: museum or visitor-center theater, planetarium, school or corporate auditorium, library. Projected program is coordinated with recorded narration, soundtrack, music stings and effects (and sometimes a live docent's introduction), lights and screen devices, repeated on a fixed daily schedule.

Outdoor / pop-up screening: park lawn, parking lot, rooftop, campus quad or community event. Portable projector, inflatable screen and PA; pre-show music playlist, live announcements or sponsor remarks on a wireless mic, start delayed until dark or until the crowd settles; ad-hoc cabling, weather and ambient noise.

Repertory or archival film-print presentation (35mm/70mm roadshow, cinematheque): overture, entr'acte and exit music coordinated with projector starts, changeovers or platter runs, curtain and house-light cues, non-sync source switching, at a presentation standard the programmer will accept.

instances.label: Daily/end-of-shift floor cleaning of a modern multiplex booth (a long narrow corridor behind the auditoria): sweeping or vacuuming dust, popcorn, paper scraps and film chips from a hard floor, working around projector pedestals, rack legs and cable runs.

Dusting and wiping the booth's surfaces and equipment exteriors: projector housings and intake vents, media server/rack faces, the workbench and shelving, light switches, and the inside face of the port glass window, using dry cloths/dusters so dust does not get into the light path.

Removing trash and clutter: emptying the booth waste bin and replacing the liner, breaking down and hauling out shipping boxes, empty film/DCP hard-drive cases and packing material, and returning tools, cleaning supplies and spare lamps to their shelves.

Cleaning the optical and airflow path as part of the booth clean: wiping lens and port-glass optical surfaces with approved solution and lens tissue, pulling and washing/vacuuming projector air filters and reinstalling them, and blowing/vacuuming dust from projector intakes and light-engine areas.

Periodic deep clean of an older or film-equipped booth: mopping, cleaning behind and underneath platters/projectors and racks, wiping down cable trays, high-dusting ledges, ducts and vents, and clearing accumulated film scraps, splice tape and oil residue.

tasks.label: Inspect movie films to ensure that they are complete and in good condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex/digital house: a feature arrives as a DCP (shipped CRU/USB drive or electronic delivery). The projectionist mounts the drive in the ingest bay or confirms the electronic transfer, checks that all reels/assets and the KDM are present and that the automatic integrity validation passed, builds the show playlist, then does a screen check in the auditorium to confirm picture, framing and sound are complete and clean before the first public show.

Repertory/art-house or festival booth: a 35mm feature arrives as 5-6 reels in shipping cans. Before the run the projectionist mounts each reel on a motorized rewind bench, winds it through by hand over a light box checking for tears, torn/strained perforations, bad splices, warping, dirt and vinegar odor, verifies reel order, head/tail leaders and footage, and writes a condition/inspection report.

Between and after screenings of a 35mm engagement: the projectionist re-checks the print for new damage (broken perforations, popped splices, scratches from the gate), inspects the platter/reel wind and leaders, verifies nothing is missing before the next show, and confirms the print is complete and intact before it is returned to the distributor.

Archive, museum or cinematheque: inspection of an old or rare acetate/nitrate print before a booking - measuring shrinkage, assessing decomposition, cataloguing every splice and perforation defect, checking frame/footage counts against records, and producing a detailed written condition report that decides whether the print may be projected.

Special-format engagement: inspecting a 70mm (or IMAX 15/70) print for a roadshow booking - very heavy large-gauge reels, magnetic/DTS sound track condition, checking every splice and perforation before building the reels or lacing the platter for a limited run.
