tasks.label: Remove full take-up reels and run film through rewinding machines to rewind projected films so they may be shown again.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repertory/art-house cinema booth running a 35mm reel-to-reel changeover show: after the screening the projectionist opens the take-up magazine, lifts off each full 2,000-ft reel, carries it to the rewind bench, mounts it on the spindle, attaches the tail/leader to an empty reel, and rewinds it head-out at controlled tension, feeling for splices and damage.

Multiplex/large venue with platter (MUT) system: at the end of a playdate the print is broken down from the platter and wound back onto shipping reels on the make-up table, and short reels/trailers are rewound on the bench for re-use.

16mm screening in a university classroom, museum theater or library AV room: small 400-1,600 ft reels removed from the projector's take-up arm and rewound on a bench rewinder or the projector's rewind function; print condition varies.

Film archive/cinematheque screening of a fragile vintage print: shrunken or brittle acetate with old tape and cement splices, rewound slowly by hand on an inspection bench with gloves, stopping at every splice or perforation damage to avoid harming an irreplaceable print.

70mm / large-format special engagement: very heavy large-diameter reels lifted off the take-up and rewound on a heavy-duty bench or platter, where mishandling risks both the print and the operator's back.

Travelling/pop-up film show (festival tent, church hall, outdoor lawn screening, microcinema): projector and portable rewinds set up on whatever table space exists, variable lighting and clearance, reels rewound on site before packing out.

sources.system: Universal X8 Automatic Slitter Rewinder (Universal Converting Equipment)
sources.title: Companies & Markets: D&M Packaging purchases a Universal X8 Automatic Slitter to support further growth
sources.claim: A commercially sold and installed slitter-rewinder automatically cuts the web at end of roll, closes and unloads the finished (full take-up) rolls, then automatically loads empty cores, positions them and attaches the web tails to the cores before restarting — the machine equivalent of removing a full take-up reel and attaching film to an empty reel to rewind.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: winding/rewinding a flexible web (plastic film, foil, paper) onto reels in a converting plant. Transfer: the physical operation is the same as rewinding motion-picture film — unloading a full wound reel, loading an empty core/reel, attaching the strip end, and winding under controlled tension — at comparable or finer web-handling precision, in a purpose-built machine enclosure.

sources.title: Smart Duplex Slitters and the Productivity Race | Packaging Strategies
sources.claim: Trade press describes the same machine as performing core loading/positioning, roll unloading and machine restart with no operator intervention, i.e., the full unload-reload-rewind cycle runs unattended.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated roll changing/rewinding of flexible web material. Transfer: establishes that removal of a full wound reel and re-winding onto a fresh reel is executed unattended at production quality in a purpose-built machine, which is the core of the projectionist's rewind cycle.

sources.system: Vision-based reel-grasping mobile manipulator (reel core ellipse detection + robotic grasp)
sources.developer: University of Bologna / Marco Carricato et al. (industrial packaging use case)
sources.title: Vision-Based Robotic Grasping of Reels for Automatic Packaging Machines (Applied Sciences)
sources.claim: A vision-guided robot manipulator autonomously recognizes reels of differing diameter and material on a deposit wagon and picks them, loading them onto an automatic packaging machine — autonomous grasping and mounting of reels that were previously handled by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: picking reels of wound material and loading them onto a machine spindle. Transfer: same object class (a flat wound reel with a central core/hub of standard bore), same manipulation — grip the reel, transport it, mount it on a spindle — which is the 'remove the full take-up reel and put it on the rewind' portion of this task.

sources.system: RML Robotic Reel Automation cell (ABB IRB7600)
sources.title: Robotic Reel Automation - RML Machinery
sources.claim: An installed industrial cell uses an ABB IRB7600 robot with vision and laser sensing to handle heavy reels and shafts automatically after operators feed reels to the cell, showing autonomous handling of large, heavy wound reels in a purpose-built enclosure.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated shafting/handling of heavy mill reels. Transfer: demonstrates that lifting a large, heavy wound reel off/onto a spindle — the physically demanding part of handling 70mm and large 35mm take-up reels — is done autonomously in a fenced industrial cell.

sources.system: IBM TS4500 tape library cartridge accessor
sources.title: Cartridge accessor - IBM Documentation (TS4500 tape library)
sources.claim: Enterprise tape libraries use a robotic cartridge accessor that autonomously removes media from drives and returns it to storage; the drive rewinds and unloads the spooled media before the robot extracts it, running continuously in production data centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling of spooled flexible media plus machine-side threading and rewinding. Transfer: the drive automatically threads the tape leader onto a take-up hub and fully rewinds the media before the robot removes it — the same sequence (rewind, then remove the reel) at very high reliability, though inside a purpose-built enclosure.

sources.title: Eiki 16mm projectors [Filmlabs Wiki]
sources.claim: Self-threading 16mm motion-picture projectors thread actual perforated film from the supply reel through the transport to the take-up reel under machine control once the film end is presented to the slot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic threading of motion-picture film through a transport onto a take-up reel. Transfer: it is the same workpiece (perforated acetate/polyester film) and the same threading step this task requires, showing machine-controlled film threading is feasible when the film end is presented as a purpose-built feed would present it.

tasks.label: Install and connect auxiliary equipment, such as microphones, amplifiers, disc playback machines, and lights.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex projection booth / equipment rack: install a new or replacement component (power amplifier, cinema audio processor, Blu-ray or disc playback machine) into the rack — lift and rack-mount it, fasten rack screws, connect AC power, and connect audio/video interconnects (XLR, RCA, HDMI/SDI, Ethernet) to the processor and projector, then power up and verify signal.

Auditorium event support in a chain cinema: set up a microphone for a pre-show introduction or post-film Q&A — place the mic stand at the front of the house, mount the mic, run/plug a mic line into a stage-box or wall input (or set a wireless receiver into the booth rack), patch it to the amplifier/processor input, bring up house lights, and sound-check levels before doors.

Special screening or film festival in the theater: set up a fuller auxiliary rig — portable PA or extra speakers, small mixer, two or three mics, a laptop/disc source feed, and podium/stage lighting — running and dressing long cable runs across the stage and house floor, taping cables down, and sound/light checking with presenters.

Small independent or art-house theater, ad-hoc hookup: connect a guest presenter's disc player or laptop to the auditorium AV chain for a pre-show clip — find/route the right HDMI and audio cables behind the rack, patch the source into the processor input, swap a bad cable or adapter, and confirm picture and sound in the auditorium.

Mobile / outdoor screening (park pop-up, drive-in, school gym, rooftop): unload gear from a van and set up on found ground — position and cable the amplifier and speakers, set up a mic and work/stage lights, run power from a generator or distant outlet, weather-protect connections, and test before the crowd arrives.

sources.system: Bright Machines Bright Robotic Cell (BRC70/BRC35) Microfactory
sources.title: Flexible, Robotic Cells Automate Back-End Assembly Processes | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: Commercial enclosed robotic assembly cells (Bright Machines Bright Robotic Cell, Fanuc/Nachi arms inside the cell) autonomously perform the mount-and-connect repertoire: placing components into housings, installing threaded fasteners, press-fitting connectors, and integrated power-up/functional testing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: back-end electronics assembly in a fixtured cell. It transfers to the E1 counterfactual of 'install and connect auxiliary equipment' because the objects (chassis, screws, multi-pin connectors), the precision (sub-millimetre mating), and the accepted output (mounted unit that passes a power-up test) are comparable; only the workpiece identity differs.

sources.system: AppMuTT connector-mating framework (industrial arm, visuotactile transformer + force control)
sources.developer: ArtiMinds Robotics / TU Braunschweig et al. (Kienle, Alt, Rayyes)
sources.title: AI-based Framework for Robust Model-Based Connector Mating in Robotic Wire Harness Installation
sources.claim: An AI/force-control framework autonomously mates electrical cable connectors (wire-harness connectors into sockets on a fixtured automotive center console) on standard industrial robot controllers, improving robustness and cycle time over hand-written programs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automotive wire-harness connector mating. The 'connect' half of this projectionist task is exactly cable-end connector insertion into a socket (XLR/RCA/HDMI vs. automotive multi-pin), at comparable precision, in a fixtured setting.

sources.system: Deep RL industrial insertion system on Rethink Sawyer arm
sources.developer: Google Brain / UC Berkeley (Schoettler et al.)
sources.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Industrial Insertion Tasks with Visual Inputs and Natural Rewards
sources.claim: A 7-DoF Sawyer robot learns and executes electric connector plug insertion (including tight, high-friction sockets requiring ~1 mm accuracy) with a fully automated, human-free training and execution loop.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: electric connector plug insertion on a benchtop fixture. Same physical act as plugging an audio/video connector into an amplifier or processor input, at equal or tighter tolerance.

sources.system: Patchy McPatchbot, Sir Patchalot, Margaret Patcher (gantry patch robots on optical distribution frames)
sources.title: DE-CIX Frankfurt 2020: Capacity increased, provisioning automated
sources.claim: Fully automated patch robots are in live production use at DE-CIX internet exchanges, physically making and changing fiber connections on purpose-built optical distribution frames without a technician touching the cables.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: patching cables between ports. It shows autonomous cable plugging is reliable enough for production, but only when the frame/panel is purpose-built around the machine — i.e. an E1-style environment inside a facility.

sources.system: Rocsys Steward / Rocsys autonomous charging robot
sources.title: Rocsys launches integrated platform to enable hands-free charging for autonomous mobility — Charged EVs
sources.claim: Commercially deployed autonomous charging robots detect a vehicle, open its port and insert/withdraw a charging connector without a human, at ports and depots (e.g. APM Terminals Maasvlakte II), handling one standardized connector at a fixed charging stall.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic connector insertion into a moderately variable target outside a fenced cell. It supports the reliability of autonomous plugging, but covers only a single standardized connector at a dedicated station, not carrying, mounting and cabling varied AV gear.

tasks.label: Observe projector operation to anticipate need to transfer operations from one projector to another.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repertory/art-house theater running a feature in 35mm from two projectors: the projectionist stands at the port glass watching the screen image for the first and second changeover cue marks, listens to the running machine, and watches lamp, framing, focus and film travel to judge exactly when the incoming projector must take over (roughly every 15-20 minutes).

Modern multiplex or dine-in cinema digital booth: the projectionist walks the booth and watches TMS/NOC status screens and auditorium windows across many screens, watching for lamp/laser faults, media-block or ingest errors, dimming or dropped frames, to anticipate the need to move a show to a backup projector or restart it on another unit before the audience notices.

Film festival or archive screening of an unfamiliar or damaged print (16mm/35mm): cue marks faint, missing, or masked, splices and shrinkage unknown, so the projectionist watches the outgoing reel and a counter/stopwatch, monitors sound and film path noise, and judges the changeover moment by hand-timed cue and picture content.

Large-format or dual-rig screening (IMAX 70mm, dual-projector 3D, or dual-machine 4K laser installations): the projectionist watches both machines' running state, sync, brightness match and fault indicators throughout the show to anticipate handing operation over to the partner machine.

Drive-in, mobile, campus, or outdoor screening with two portable projectors set up for the night: variable light, weather, and improvised sight-lines while the operator watches the screen and machines to anticipate the reel changeover.

tasks.label: Prepare film inspection reports, attendance sheets, and log books.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Splice separate film reels, advertisements, and movie trailers together to form a feature-length presentation on one continuous reel.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial cinema booth, weekly 35mm print build: five to seven 2,000-ft feature reels arrive in cans, are wound onto a platter on a rewind bench and tape-spliced in order with the policy trailer, ad reel and several trailers; projectionist checks head/tail leaders, frame-line splices, correct order and cue marks. Takes 30-45 minutes.

Weekly changeover of advertising and trailers on an already-built program: projectionist finds the existing splices on the wound platter, cuts out expired trailers/ads, splices the newly booked ones in the required order, and re-winds the program back onto the platter.

Repair splicing on a print in service: a break, damaged perforations or a failed splice mid-run; projectionist trims the damaged frames to a frame line, makes a new tape splice, re-threads and restarts, often under showtime pressure with a partly wound platter.

Repertory, museum or festival booth building an older or rare print: shrunken acetate mixed with polyester, existing cement and tape splices, careful inspection for damage, clear archival tape splices only, sometimes assembled for reel-to-reel changeover rather than a platter.

Large-format build (70mm or IMAX 15/70): dozens of heavy individual reels shipped separately, spliced and wound over many hours by a team at a dedicated splicing/winding bench onto a very large platter, with zero tolerance for scratches or a failed splice.

sources.system: Manual hand-splicing by theater projection staff (no robotic system)
sources.title: Why 1960s technology makes seeing 'The Odyssey' in 70mm IMAX so difficult
sources.claim: As of 2026, 70mm IMAX prints of 'The Odyssey' are shipped in portions and spliced together by hand over several hours by theater staff onto a giant platter — the task is performed manually, with no automated assembly system.
sources.transferJustification: Directly describes the task instance (assembling shipped reels into one continuous presentation reel) and shows it is done by human hands, not machines.

sources.system: Manual splicing by Science Museum projection team (no robotic system)
sources.title: A projectionist's guide to Oppenheimer IMAX 70mm — Science Museum Blog
sources.claim: A large-format feature print delivered as 53 separate reels was spliced, taped and wound into a single print by a team of skilled human projectionists over 16 hours.
sources.transferJustification: Same task, large-format variant; establishes that the state of practice is fully manual assembly.

sources.system: Manual print build on rewind bench and platter (no robotic system)
sources.title: How We Show You Movies • Ragtag Cinema
sources.claim: Standard cinema print building — winding reels onto the platter in the correct order and tape-splicing them together — is described as a manual booth operation taking a head projectionist 30-45 minutes.
sources.transferJustification: Directly describes the mainstream instance of this task and confirms it is a hand operation by a projectionist.

sources.system: Smart Shot semi-automatic heat seal film splicer
sources.title: Smart Shot Film Splicer from Source Two, Inc.
sources.claim: The most capable commercial motion-picture-film splicing machine found is a semi-automatic bench heat-seal splicer for processing labs: it positions and seals a single presented joint, but an operator must feed and initiate every splice; it does not sequence, wind, or assemble a program.
sources.transferJustification: Closest machine to the splicing sub-step on perforated 16/35mm film; cited to show that even purpose-built film splicing machinery is operator-fed and covers only one joint, not the whole build.

sources.system: Butler Automatic SP1 automatic film splicer
sources.title: Butler Automatic — SP1 Automatic Splicer
sources.claim: Fully automatic web splicers used in packaging lines join an expiring roll to a new roll without stopping, but only after an operator has manually prepared the splice on the new roll; they make unregistered lap splices on disposable packaging film.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (joining two flexible film webs in a purpose-built line); cited to show its limits — operator splice preparation, no frame-line/perforation registration, no program sequencing — so it does not transfer to assembling a feature print.

sources.system: Manual tape splicing practice (Sprocket School guidance)
sources.title: Splicing — Sprocket School
sources.claim: Archival exhibition standards require projectionists to make clear archival tape splices by hand and to inspect and recognize existing splice types on old prints, a judgment-and-dexterity task with no machine substitute cited.
sources.transferJustification: Describes the quality standard the assembled print must meet in archival/repertory instances, showing the inspection and splice-type judgment required.

roles.title: Ushers, Lobby Attendants, and Ticket Takers
roles.description: Assist patrons at entertainment events by performing duties, such as collecting admission tickets and passes from patrons, assisting in finding seats, searching for lost articles, and helping patrons locate such facilities as restrooms and telephones.

tasks.label: Sell or collect admission tickets, passes, or facility memberships from patrons at entertainment events.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Entry gate of a large stadium or arena on event day: a ticket taker stands at a gate position in a fixed entry plaza/concourse, scanning barcode/QR tickets on phones and print-at-home sheets from a dense stream of arriving fans, redirecting wrong-gate or already-scanned tickets, working in whatever weather the outdoor gate has.

Movie theater: box-office/lobby staff sell walk-up tickets by card or cash and print them, then a ticket taker at the podium scans or tears the ticket, hands back the stub, and points patrons toward the auditorium; steady indoor lobby, predictable layout.

Admission desk or booth at a museum, zoo, aquarium, or theme park: selling general-admission and timed tickets, upselling and processing memberships, taking card or cash payment, printing tickets/wristbands/member cards, and scanning them at the entry turnstile.

Door of a small club, community theater, or performing-arts house: collecting paper or mobile tickets and will-call names at a folding table, selling remaining tickets at the door for cash, issuing wristbands or hand stamps for re-entry, with irregular arrival surges before curtain.

Temporary outdoor gate at a fair, festival, or fairground event: a fenced entry lane set up for the run of the event, scanning wristbands/mobile tickets and selling day passes at a portable booth, on grass or gravel, in sun, wind, or rain.

Event staged in a public space (park concert, street fair, fireworks grandstand, parade viewing area): staff sell tickets from a cash box or handheld and check passes among patrons on a sidewalk or lawn with no fixed entry structure.

sources.developer: Axess AG / Diamond Peak Ski Resort
sources.title: RFID Gates - Diamond Peak Ski Resort
sources.claim: Axess motorized RFID gates at Diamond Peak Ski Resort read a guest's season pass or lift ticket and open the gate automatically, admitting the pass holder without any staff scanning the credential.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: lift-access pass validation. Same act as collecting an admission pass at an entertainment venue — read the patron's credential, decide admit/deny, and physically open the barrier — performed unattended at an institution-controlled outdoor resort.

sources.title: Denver Broncos speed up entry with new walk-through detectors - Stadium Tech Report
sources.claim: The Denver Broncos deployed Axess self-scanning ticketing pedestals at Empower Field entry points, letting fans validate their own tickets by scan or NFC instead of having a ticket taker do it, with a staffer nearby only to help unfamiliar fans.

sources.system: Alvarado UltraQ Pedestal / UltraQ Portable Pedestal
sources.title: Alvarado UltraQ Pedestal enhances fan experiences worldwide
sources.claim: Alvarado's UltraQ pedestals let guests self-validate tickets for venue entry; the portable, battery-powered, Wi-Fi version can be dropped at any entry point, and Alvarado hardware scanned over a million fans on a single recent tour.

sources.title: AMC Kiosk - AMC Ticketing Kiosks (Kiosk Industry case study)
sources.claim: AMC Theatres deployed Pyramid polytouch self-service ticketing kiosks — touchscreen with thermal ticket printer, card reader for payment, and barcode/QR scanner — across its theater circuit, replacing older-generation kiosks for lobby ticket purchases.

sources.developer: Wildlife Conservation Society / Central Park Zoo
sources.title: FAQs - Central Park Zoo
sources.claim: The Central Park Zoo sells walk-up admission tickets through an on-site self-serve kiosk as an alternative to the staffed ticket window.

sources.claim: Climate Pledge Arena entry was automated with the Axess SMART SCANNER 600 integrated with Amazon One palm biometrics and Ticketmaster, admitting ticket holders by palm scan rather than a staff ticket check.

sources.claim: Semnox Parafait self-service ticketing kiosks at amusement and theme parks sell admissions and physically print and issue the resulting tickets or RFID/barcode wristbands from blank stock loaded in the machine.

sources.claim: Museum self-service kiosks handle general-admission and special-exhibition ticket purchases and also sell membership programs, reducing lines at staffed admission counters.

tasks.label: Clean facilities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cinema auditorium turnover between showings: usher enters after the crowd leaves and, within a 10-20 minute window, pulls cups and popcorn buckets from cupholders and seats, bags loose wrappers and 3D glasses, sweeps spilled popcorn from between fixed rows and down the sloped aisle/stairs, and spot-wipes sticky seats and armrests before the next audience is admitted.

Lobby, concession and concourse floor care: sweeping, dust-mopping or vacuuming large open carpeted and hard-floor areas, and damp-mopping/scrubbing them, typically before opening or between show breaks with patrons and stanchions present.

Restroom checks and cleaning during operating hours: wiping sinks, counters and mirrors, cleaning/flushing toilets and urinals, picking up floor trash, and mopping or damp-cleaning the restroom floor.

Post-event tidy of a live venue or stadium seating section: walking assigned rows collecting programs, cups, bottles and food waste from seats, seat backs and under seats, bagging it, flipping seats up and wiping obvious spills before the venue is locked.

Waste and supply servicing: emptying and relining lobby, concourse and restroom trash/recycling receptacles, hauling full bags to the compactor or dumpster, and restocking restroom paper towels, toilet paper and ....

Mid-event spot response: dispatched to a reported mess during a show or game - a spilled soda in an aisle or between seat rows, dropped popcorn, broken glass, or vomit - placing a wet-floor sign, cleaning and sanitizing the spot quickly and quietly, then returning to post.

sources.title: CVG Airport starts use of Avidbots Neo floor-scrubbing robot
sources.claim: Avidbots Neo, a fully autonomous floor-scrubbing robot, was put into service cleaning terminal floors at Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport, navigating around people, luggage and furniture during operations.
sources.transferJustification: Terminal floor scrubbing is the same work as lobby/concourse floor care in a venue: large open human-traffic floors, hard surfaces, debris and spills, cleaned during operating hours.

sources.title: Avidbots Designs Fully Autonomous Cleaning Robots for Airports and Hospitals
sources.claim: Avidbots' autonomous floor scrubbers are in routine commercial service across many categories of structured human facilities worldwide.

sources.system: BrainOS-powered scrubbers and vacuums (Whiz, Tennant X6 ROVR)
sources.title: Brain Corp: Robots, AI, and autonomous technology for smarter operations
sources.claim: Brain Corp's BrainOS powers a large commercial fleet of autonomous scrubbers and vacuums (including the Whiz carpet vacuum and Tennant scrubbers) operating in indoor public spaces with little human intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Carpet vacuuming and hard-floor scrubbing in retail/public indoor spaces is the same operation as vacuuming and mopping a theater lobby or concourse floor.

sources.title: Somatic - Autonomous Bathroom Cleaning Robots
sources.claim: Somatic's BCR is a commercially offered autonomous bathroom-cleaning robot deployed in hospitals and airports; its spec sheet lists spraying primary and glass cleaner, wet-vacuuming, scrubbing, blow-drying, squeegeeing, a trash pickup tool, door opening, toilet seat up/down and flushing, with autonomous water refill and recharging.
sources.transferJustification: High-traffic airport and hospital restrooms are equivalent to venue public restrooms in fixtures, layout and soil; the robot performs the same fixture, glass, floor and trash-pickup steps an usher performs on a restroom check.

sources.title: Those viral bathroom-cleaning bots won't be saving our butts anytime soon
sources.claim: Reporting on Somatic's robot confirms it works unattended in a medical facility's restrooms but that restocking consumables and taking trash out of the building still require human staff.

sources.title: Gausium Phantas AI-Powered Floor Cleaning Robot
sources.claim: Gausium's compact Phantas cleaning robot autonomously sweeps, scrubs, vacuums and mops in furniture-dense commercial spaces and can detect soil and perform spot cleaning, but vendor guidance notes it excludes waste it cannot handle safely, such as large liquid spills.
sources.transferJustification: Spot cleaning of soiled floor patches in furniture-dense commercial interiors is the closest available analogue to a venue lobby floor clean-up.

sources.system: Autonomous scrubbers/vacuums for entertainment venues (RobotLAB portfolio)
sources.title: Robots for Entertainment Venues & Attractions
sources.claim: A robotics integrator selling cleaning robots to entertainment venues states that autonomous scrubbers and vacuums cover the lobby and concession areas while human staff still perform row-by-row pickup in the seating area after every show.

sources.title: Figure humanoid robot cleans cluttered living room in new video demo
sources.claim: Figure AI released a demonstration of its Figure 03 humanoid autonomously ... cluttered living room using its Helix 02 system; this is a demo in a home mock-up, not a deployed venue capability with turnover-speed throughput.
sources.transferJustification: Tidying loose objects is the nearest manipulation analogue to clearing cups and popcorn buckets from theater rows, but it is a single-room demo without the throughput, seat-row access or reliability a turnover requires.

tasks.label: Provide assistance with patrons' special needs, such as helping those with wheelchairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Arena/theater/cinema: a patron arrives in their own powered wheelchair or scooter. The usher greets them, checks the ticket, and escorts them along the step-free route (concourse, ramp, elevator) to the accessible seating platform, confirms the wheelchair space and companion seat are clear, and points out the accessible restroom. No hands-on physical help is needed.

Same escort, but hands-on work is required: pushing the house manual wheelchair up a ramp or over a threshold, pulling open heavy manual doors, flipping up or removing a companion seat, threading a packed pre-show concourse, folding and stowing the patron's chair beside the seat.

A patron who can stand and self-transfer but cannot walk the distance asks for a house wheelchair. The usher fetches it, the patron gets in, the usher conveys them from the box office/drop-off to their seating row, and returns the chair to storage; the trip is repeated at the end of the show.

A frail, elderly, or injured patron needs an arm to lean on down a steeply raked aisle or a stair, steadying while they lower into and later rise from the seat, their cane/walker taken and stowed, and their coat or bag carried.

A blind or low-vision patron (sometimes with a guide dog) is met at the door and guided through the lobby to their exact seat, told about the route, row, exits and restroom, and collected again at intermission or at the end.

Guest-services window: issue an assistive listening or open-caption device, booster seat, or sensory kit — take an ID/deposit, pick the right unit from the charging rack, hand it over and show the patron how to wear and tune it, then collect it after the show and return it to the charger.

Unpredictable special-need situations: relocating a distressed autistic patron to a quiet area, assisting a patron who becomes ill or falls, or shepherding disabled patrons through an unplanned evacuation or a crowd surge at egress.

sources.system: WHILL Autonomous Driving System (with Unifi Aviation)
sources.title: Unifi Launches WHILL Autonomous Wheelchair Service at Detroit Metro Airport
sources.claim: WHILL's self-driving wheelchairs are in commercial airport service (DTW, LAX, MIA, SEA, AMS, YWG): a passenger with reduced mobility boards at a station and the chair autonomously drives them to their gate on pre-mapped routes, then returns to base by itself.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: airport wheelchair-assist attendants conveying a mobility-limited traveler to a destination inside a crowded public facility. Same object (a seated adult in a wheelchair), same precision (door-width clearances, pedestrian traffic), and an equivalent institution-run concourse, so it carries over to conveying a patron from a venue lobby to accessible seating.

sources.title: WHILL Launches Autonomous Services at Munich Airport
sources.claim: At Munich Airport the same WHILL autonomous service still relies on human staff to meet the passenger, assist with boarding and stow carry-on items; the robot performs only the driving leg, and airports state passengers needing more hands-on help keep traditional attendant service.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above; cited to bound the capability — the autonomous portion is conveyance only, not the hands-on boarding, stowing and transfer help an usher gives.

sources.developer: WHILL, Inc. / National Museum of Ethnology (Minpaku)
sources.title: National Museum of Ethnology (Minpaku) – Attractions and Highlights | Osaka Info
sources.claim: A WHILL autonomous driving vehicle is offered to visitors inside the main exhibition hall of Japan's National Museum of Ethnology, i.e. an autonomous personal-mobility service running inside a public cultural venue rather than only in airports.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: providing a mobility-impaired visitor with self-driving transport through an exhibition venue, the same service an usher provides with a house wheelchair in a theater or arena.

sources.title: Miraikan Accessibility Lab. | Miraikan – The National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation

tasks.label: Maintain order and ensure adherence to safety rules.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Live theater / concert hall auditorium during a performance: usher posted at an aisle in dim light watches the seated house, stops flash photography and recording, quiets talking, keeps aisle steps and exit rows clear of coats and bags, prevents patrons moving to better seats, holds latecomers at the rear until a break and walks them in, escalates persistent offenders to house management.

Stadium or arena seating section during a game or large concert: usher at the section portal enforces no standing in aisles or crossovers, checks that fans are in their ticketed section, blocks access to restricted areas (field, press, premium levels), watches for intoxicated, smoking or fighting fans and radios security, keeps stairways clear during dense ingress/egress, all under noise, crowding and variable lighting.

Movie theater: periodic walkthrough sweeps of auditoriums and concourse checking for talking/phone use, vaping, unauthorized recording, feet on seats, propped or blocked emergency exit doors, unaccompanied minors after hours, and disruptive groups; verbal correction and ejection with manager backup.

Lobby, entrance and queue control before and after an event: managing stanchioned lines, directing crowd flow through doors, enforcing prohibited-item, bag, smoking and re-entry rules, keeping fire lanes, doorways and stairwells clear, and preventing patrons from entering closed or restricted areas.

Urgent safety incident or evacuation in the venue: fire alarm, medical emergency, power failure or severe-weather hold; usher directs patrons to the nearest exit, opens and staffs exit doors, clears the path of obstructions, keeps the crowd from bottlenecking, assists mobility-impaired patrons, and holds people back from a hazard area until responders arrive.

Outdoor festival, fairground or street-event site: temporary layout on grass or pavement with variable terrain, weather and lighting, crowd pressing against barricades near a stage, patrons spilling onto adjoining public ground; attendant keeps aisles and emergency lanes open, stops climbing on structures and fence-jumping, and manages surging crowds.

sources.title: The Force — Autonomous Security Force | Knightscope (K5 product page)
sources.claim: Knightscope's K5 is a commercially sold, fully autonomous patrol robot providing surveillance, physical presence/deterrence and remote monitoring on properties; it detects and reports and can broadcast automated voice warnings, but it does not physically intervene with people or secure compliance with venue rules.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous security patrol in the same class of venues. It transfers only for passive observation and deterrence; the usher task additionally requires identifying specific rule violations among seated patrons and obtaining compliance, which the K5 escalates to human staff rather than performing.

sources.title: Using Robots for Security in Sports Venues | Athletic Business
sources.claim: Knightscope patrol robots have been deployed at large sporting venues including the Sacramento Kings' Golden 1 Center, where the machine functions as a roving surveillance/deterrence presence, not as crowd-order staff.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: venue security patrol in an arena, the same setting as the stadium usher instance. It substantiates autonomous presence in the concourse but not enforcement of seating/safety rules on patrons.

sources.title: NYPD 'robocop' no longer patrolling following end of pilot program | Police1
sources.claim: In the closest people-dense public-facility trial (Times Square subway station, a crowded transit concourse comparable to a venue concourse), the K5 could not operate unattended: it required two police officers with it at all times and the pilot ended without redeployment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: crowd-facing patrol in a busy public facility. It shows the limit of the transfer — even monitoring presence among dense crowds needed continuous human escort, so it cannot substitute for an usher maintaining order.

sources.title: AWS, Seqsense Team on Autonomous Security Robot Development | IoT World Today
sources.claim: SEQSENSE's SQ-2 autonomously patrols public-facing buildings including airports and shopping centers in Japan, navigating among people and reporting anomalies to a remote guard center; its role is detection and reporting, not directing or correcting people.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: indoor autonomous security patrol in structured public facilities (E2). Transfer covers navigation and surveillance in crowded human venues, but not violation-specific intervention, aisle clearing, or evacuation direction.

sources.title: LG Targets AI and Robotics for Intuitive Lifestyle | LG press release
sources.claim: LG's CLOi GuideBot operates in service at Incheon International Airport, autonomously escorting passengers to their gates among crowds — demonstrating patron-facing autonomous navigation and guidance in a structured facility, without any rule-enforcement or intervention function.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: guiding patrons in a crowded structured facility, an usher-adjacent duty. It transfers for wayfinding, but provides no evidence of detecting rule violations, obtaining compliance, clearing aisles, or emergency crowd direction.

tasks.label: Examine tickets or passes to verify authenticity, using criteria such as color or date issued.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex cinema: ticket taker at the podium receives a printed box-office ticket or a phone barcode, checks film/auditorium/showtime and date, confirms it is not a duplicate or a previous day's stub, tears/marks it and admits the patron. Indoor lobby, steady bursts of arrivals.

Stadium or arena entry gate: high-volume verification of mobile SafeTix-style tickets, print-at-home PDFs, season-ticket cards and staff/media credentials at turnstile banks; must catch already-scanned, wrong-date, wrong-gate and counterfeit copies during a 60-90 minute ingress peak, outdoors or in a covered concourse.

Performing arts theater, concert hall or club: usher checks each patron's ticket at the auditorium door (and sometimes again in the aisle) for correct performance date/time, section and seat; mix of barcoded box-office tickets, will-call and mobile tickets; dim lobby lighting, short pre-curtain rush.

Theme park, water park, zoo or museum admission gate: verify dated/timed-entry tickets, annual or season passes tied to a photo, member cards and ski-style day passes; check the pass is valid for that date and blockout, then admit through the gate.

Fenced outdoor festival, fairground or racetrack gate: promoter-controlled entry lanes with temporary fencing; verify RFID wristbands, barcoded day tickets and color-coded VIP/artist/crew credentials; weather, dust, crowd surges.

Small community and street-level events plus problem cases: pop-up admission table on a sidewalk, field or church hall; hand-issued or color-coded paper passes, comps, rain-checks and hand stamps with no machine-readable code; also roving spot-checks in premium areas and inspection of a suspected counterfeit (paper stock, ink, date issued) with escalation of the patron.

tasks.label: Guide patrons to exits or provide other instructions or assistance in case of emergency.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Full evacuation of a seated-audience venue (cinema, theater, arena) on a fire alarm, bomb threat or severe-weather order: usher holds an aisle post, verbally and physically directs a crowd of hundreds up aisles to the nearest legal exit, pushes crash-bar doors open and holds them, sweeps rows, aisles and restrooms for stragglers, and blocks re-entry, amid alarm noise, emergency lighting and moving people.

Medical emergency in the seating bowl or concourse (collapse, seizure, fall): usher moves nearby patrons back and clears a working space and aisle, calls it in, meets EMS at the door and leads them through crowded concourses to the patient, and helps walk or wheel the patient out to a first-aid room or ambulance exit.

Assisting patrons who cannot self-evacuate: wheelchair users, elderly or injured patrons, unaccompanied children, intoxicated or panicked guests. Usher physically supports or steadies the person, moves a wheelchair, uses an evacuation chair on stairs (elevators disabled), takes them to an area of refuge or street-level exit, and stays with them until relieved.

Localized incident during an event (smoke or burning smell, fight, spill, lighting/power failure, unruly patron, shelter-in-place order): usher relocates or evacuates one section, staffs a post to keep patrons away from the hazard, and repeats instructions to confused patrons in a loud, dark, crowded space.

Routine emergency-preparedness duties performed around patrons: giving pre-show exit briefings or answering 'where is the nearest exit' questions, keeping exit routes, doors and aisles clear of bags, strollers and standing patrons, taking assigned posts during drills, and directing an orderly early exit when a show is stopped.

sources.system: Teleoperated four-wheeled evacuation guidance robot (Wagner lab)
sources.developer: Pennsylvania State University (Nayyar, Wagner et al.)
sources.title: Learning Evacuee Models from Robot-Guided Emergency Evacuation Experiments
sources.claim: State-of-the-art robot-guided emergency evacuation experiments (human subjects, simulated smoke-alarm emergency in an office/lab building) still rely on a teleoperated ground robot because fully autonomous indoor evacuation guidance remains too hard.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the task: a robot leading a person to a building exit during a simulated emergency. It shows the capability exists only under continuous human teleoperation in a controlled office setting, not autonomously in a public venue.

sources.system: Evacuation guidance robots (shepherding / actuated traffic-cop concepts)

sources.claim: A review of the robot-guided evacuation research program states that building an autonomous robot that shepherds evacuees to exits during an emergency is technically ...; the work is framed as an HRI research paradigm, not a fielded capability.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (guiding people to exits in an emergency); establishes that no autonomous system reliably performs it, even in mapped buildings.

sources.claim: Autonomous guide robots are deployed in structured public facilities where they escort individual travellers to a destination in the terminal, under normal (non-emergency) conditions.

sources.claim: Self-driving personal mobility chairs are commercially deployed in airport terminals, carrying passengers who need assistance from check-in through security to the gate on pre-mapped routes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: moving a mobility-limited person through a public facility. It covers only self-boarding passengers on flat pre-mapped routes in normal operation; not stair descent, evacuation chairs, or physically supporting an injured or panicked patron.

sources.developer: IntBot / San Jose Mineta International Airport
sources.title: US airport deploys humanoid robot to greet and help passengers

sources.transferJustification: Related task: giving patrons directions in a public facility. Establishes that the deployed state of the art is a fixed-post information robot, which cannot execute the mobile, physical, crowd-facing parts of emergency guidance.

tasks.label: Search for lost articles or for parents of lost children.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Movie theater or performing-arts venue between showings/at close: usher walks the rows with a flashlight checking seats, seat backs, cup holders and floors for items left behind (phones, keys, glasses, coats, bags), separates them from popcorn and litter, and logs them at lost-and-found.

Patron at an arena, stadium or theater reports losing a phone, wallet, jewelry or coat at a seat; the usher goes to the reported section, searches under and around seats amid litter and other patrons (sometimes mid-event with the lights down), asks neighbors, and hands the item back or logs it.

Item lost elsewhere in the venue - lobby, restroom, concession line, concourse, or parking lot; usher retraces the patron's route, checks tables, floors, ledges and trash receptacles, and coordinates by radio with other staff and guest services.

A lost child is found alone in a concourse or aisle; the usher takes charge of the child, calms them, gets a description of the adult, escorts the child to guest services, scans the crowd/nearby sections for the parent, and verifies the adult's identity before releasing the child.

A parent reports a missing child; the usher searches the venue - darkened auditorium, restrooms, play areas, exits - for a child matching the description while radioing other staff, then brings the child back and reunites the family.

sources.title: Amazon introduces Sparrow—a state-of-the-art robot that handles millions of diverse products
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously detects, singulates and picks individual products out of large assortments of diverse goods inside fenced fulfillment-center cells, at production reliability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: item-level picking of a specified product from mixed inventory. Under the E1 counterfactual the lost-article instance reduces to recognizing and retrieving one designated small personal object (phone, wallet, glasses) from presented material in a purpose-built cell, which is what Sparrow does with comparable objects and precision.

sources.title: AMP's Horowitz on Bringing AI to the Recycling World
sources.claim: AMP Robotics' AI-guided Cortex sorting robots autonomously recognize and pick target objects out of mixed, cluttered waste streams in materials-recovery facilities at high accuracy and speed, including e-waste and construction debris streams.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: separating designated objects from mixed debris on a conveyor in a purpose-built cell. This matches the E1 form of a post-show sweep - distinguishing a patron's belongings from popcorn, cups and wrappers and extracting them intact - with comparable object variety and precision.

sources.title: OK-Robot: What Really Matters in Integrating Open-Knowledge Models for Robotics
sources.claim: State-of-the-art open-vocabulary mobile manipulation that fetches a named object in real, unstructured rooms succeeds only about 58% of the time, far below the reliability an usher's employer would accept.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching a named object in a human-occupied space. It is the closest published analogue to searching seats or a lobby for a described lost article; its success rate shows the capability is not at worker quality outside purpose-built settings.

sources.title: Roborock Saros Z70 Review: A Robot Vacuum with a Mechanical Arm? | Vacuum Wars
sources.claim: The only commercially sold mobile robot with an arm that picks objects off the floor works on a narrow trained set of light items and succeeds roughly half the time.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously spotting and retrieving small items left on the floor of a human-occupied room. Shows that in-situ object retrieval outside a purpose-built cell is limited to trained categories and unreliable.

sources.system: Autonomous scrubbers/vacuums in cinemas and venues

sources.title: Cobalt intelligent indoor security robot | Security Info Watch
sources.claim: Autonomous indoor security robots patrol institution-controlled facilities on mapped routes and raise alerts for humans, but their function is detection and escalation, not retrieving objects or taking charge of people.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous patrol of a structured human facility. It establishes that navigation of an E2 venue is solved, while the search-identify-retrieve and child-custody parts of this task are not addressed by any patrol robot.

sources.title: Angsa Robotics - Munich Startup
sources.claim: An autonomous outdoor robot locates and removes small litter items from grass and gravel at parks, green spaces and open-air festival sites, operating around people.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously finding and collecting small objects across a venue's grounds. It shows area-sweep collection exists outdoors, but it collects litter indiscriminately into a bin rather than identifying, preserving and returning a patron's specific lost article.

instances.label: Performing-arts venue (theater, concert hall, opera house) intermission refreshment counter: the usher/attendant staffs a lobby bar selling wine, beer, soft drinks, bottled water, coffee and packaged sweets, taking card payment and clearing a queue of patrons inside a 15-20 minute intermission.

Stadium/arena concession stand or portable cart during breaks between periods: multi-item menu (fountain sodas, draft beer with ID check, hot dogs, nachos, popcorn, candy), cash and card POS, heavy rush-hour queues, food kept hot and orders bagged and handed across a counter.

Small or community venue (school auditorium, community theater, minor-league or amateur venue): improvised folding-table refreshment stand with a coffee urn, cooler of cans, homemade baked goods and a cash box; the usher sets it up, sells during intermission, then tears it down.

Press box / suite refreshment runs: attendant takes verbal orders from reporters and press-box guests, walks to the commissary or concession (often another level, via stairs or elevator), gathers drinks and food on a tray, returns and distributes items at individual desks while play continues.

Stand setup, restocking and closing: hauling cases of drinks and bags of ice, loading coolers, cup and condiment dispensers, refilling popcorn/candy displays mid-event, wiping counters, counting and closing out the cash drawer and securing product.

tasks.label: Count and record number of tickets collected.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multiplex movie theater: ticket taker at the podium collects/scans printed and mobile tickets for each showtime; at the end of the shift the admissions collected per auditorium/showtime are counted and recorded on the usher report and reconciled against box-office sales. Indoor lobby, fixed layout, chain-standard equipment.

Live theater / performing arts venue: ticket takers tear paper tickets and drop the stubs in a box or bucket; at intermission or after the house closes, the stubs are counted by hand and the attendance number is recorded on the house/settlement report and reconciled to the box-office count. Loose, irregularly torn paper stubs, mixed comps and paid stubs.

Stadium/arena gate crew: each gate validates tickets via turnstiles or handheld scanners; per-gate scan counts, plus collected paper comp/will-call stubs, are tallied at the end of entry and recorded for the event attendance and revenue reconciliation report. Large concourse, crowd surges, institution-controlled premises.

Theme park, waterpark, museum, or family entertainment center attraction: admission media (barcoded tickets, wristbands, ride tickets) collected at the entry or attraction; totals per gate/attraction/shift counted and recorded for attendance and auditing. Indoor/outdoor but institution-controlled grounds with fixed gate lines.

Outdoor or pop-up event gate: county fair, street festival, school carnival, church hall show or seasonal haunted attraction; paper tickets torn into a bucket at a folding-table gate, counted at the end of the night and recorded on a tally/cash-reconciliation sheet. Layout differs event to event, variable weather and lighting, no fixed installed equipment.
